al-swearengen.bio: Ellis Albert Swearengen was born in Oskaloosa, Iowa, and arrived in Deadwood in 1876, where he opened the Cricket Saloon and then the Gem Variety Theater in 1877. The Gem was Deadwood's most notorious brothel and theater. Swearengen recruited women with promises of respectable jobs and then forced them into prostitution, and he was known for beating them. It burned twice; after the second fire in 1899 he left Deadwood, broke. On November 15, 1904, he was found dead in a Denver street with a head wound, probably murdered. The HBO series 'Deadwood' made him famous again a century later.

alexander-mcsween.bio:
Alexander Anderson McSween was born in Canada to a Scottish family and, by his widow's account, was a Presbyterian preacher in his youth. He studied law in St. Louis, married Susan Hummer in Kansas in 1873 and came to Lincoln in 1875 to work as a lawyer for Murphy and Dolan's House. He soon broke with them and went into business with John Tunstall.

A dispute over a life insurance payout he was handling gave the House a legal weapon against him, and the attempt to seize his and Tunstall's property led to Tunstall's murder. McSween became the leader of the Regulators but was not a fighting man himself. In July 1878 his house in Lincoln was surrounded and burned in the Battle of Lincoln. On the last night he walked out of the burning house, unarmed, and was shot dead. His widow, Susan, went on to become one of the most successful cattle ranchers in New Mexico.

andrew-roberts.bio:
Andrew 'Buckshot' Roberts was a small, older man, said to be a former soldier, whose nickname came from a load of buckshot still lodged in his body that kept him from raising his right arm to his shoulder. He had a small ranch near Lincoln and had ridden with the posse that killed John Tunstall, which put him on the Regulators' list.

On April 4, 1878, the Regulators found him at Blazer's Mill. He refused to surrender. Charlie Bowdre shot him through the middle, but Roberts kept fighting, wounding George Coe and John Middleton and, from inside Dr. Blazer's office, killing Dick Brewer with a shot through the head. He died the next day and was buried beside Brewer.

legends.text: Fought Regulators alone

annie-oakley.bio:
Phoebe Ann Mosey was born in a cabin in Darke County, Ohio. After her father died, her family fell into poverty, and as a child she was sent to the county poor farm and then hired out to a family that abused her. She learned to shoot as a girl and sold the game she hunted to shops in Greenville and Cincinnati, earning enough to help pay off her mother's farm mortgage.

As a young woman she beat touring marksman Frank Butler in a shooting match, and they married. Taking the stage name Annie Oakley, she became the star of Buffalo Bill's Wild West in 1885 and toured with it for 16 years, including Europe. Sitting Bull, who toured with the show, adopted her and called her 'Little Sure Shot.' She could split a playing card edge-on and shoot a dime tossed in the air.

In 1903 Hearst newspapers falsely reported she had been arrested for stealing to buy cocaine. She spent years suing and won nearly all her cases. She taught thousands of women to shoot and offered to raise a company of women sharpshooters for the Spanish-American War. She died in Greenville, Ohio, in November 1926. Frank Butler died 18 days later.
incidents: Star of Buffalo Bill's Wild West

legends.text: Sitting Bull named her 'Little Sure Shot'

annie-roberts.bio: Annie Roberts co-owned the Bisbee House restaurant with her husband. On December 8, 1883, she stepped outside when she heard the shooting and was shot in the back by one of the robbers. She was pregnant and died that evening along with her unborn child. Her death, more than any other, turned public anger against the Bisbee raiders and led to the lynching of John Heath.

bass-reeves.bio:
Bass Reeves was born into slavery in Crawford County, Arkansas, and taken to Texas by his enslaver, William Reeves. During the Civil War he escaped to Indian Territory, where he lived among the Cherokee, Creek and Seminole and learned their languages and the land. After the war he farmed in Arkansas.

In 1875 Judge Isaac Parker's court at Fort Smith hired him as a deputy U.S. marshal, making him one of the first Black deputy marshals west of the Mississippi. He couldn't read or write, so he memorized his warrants. Over 32 years he is credited with more than 3,000 arrests and killed 14 men in the line of duty, and he was known for disguises and patience. He even arrested his own son for murdering his wife.

When Oklahoma became a state in 1907 he joined the Muskogee police force. He died in 1910. Some historians have suggested he inspired the Lone Ranger, though there is no direct evidence. His grave in Muskogee is unmarked and its location is lost.

legends.text: Inspiration for the Lone Ranger

bat-masterson.bio:
Bartholomew 'Bat' Masterson was born in Quebec and grew up on farms in New York, Illinois and Kansas, where his family settled near Wichita. With his brothers Ed and Jim he worked on railroad grading crews and hunted buffalo. In June 1874, at 20, he survived the Second Battle of Adobe Walls in the Texas Panhandle, where a few dozen hunters held off hundreds of Comanche and Cheyenne warriors. In 1876, in Sweetwater, Texas, he was shot in the pelvis in a fight in which Corporal Melvin King and a dance hall girl named Mollie Brennan were killed; he walked with a cane for a time afterward.

In Dodge City he served as a deputy and in 1877 was elected Ford County sheriff, capturing train robbers including Dave Rudabaugh. His brother Ed, the Dodge City marshal, was killed in 1878. In 1879 he led the Santa Fe Railroad's hired guns in the Royal Gorge War. He came back to Dodge more than once to back up his brother Jim and his friend Luke Short, and he helped keep Doc Holliday from being extradited to Arizona in 1882.

He spent the 1880s and 1890s in Denver as a gambler, saloon man and boxing promoter, then moved to New York in 1902. Theodore Roosevelt appointed him a deputy U.S. marshal, and he became a sports columnist and editor at the New York Morning Telegraph. He died at his desk in October 1921. His last column ended with a wry line about the rich getting ice in the summer and the poor getting it in the winter.

belle-starr.bio:
Myra Maybelle Shirley was born near Carthage, Missouri, to a well-off family and attended a girls' academy. Her brother Bud rode with Confederate bushwhackers and was killed in 1864, and the family moved to Scyene, Texas. In 1866 she married Jim Reed, who turned outlaw and was killed in 1874. She knew the James and Younger brothers, and rumors that Cole Younger fathered her daughter Pearl have never been proven.

In 1880 she married Sam Starr, a Cherokee, and they settled at a place on the Canadian River she called Younger's Bend, which became known as a hideout for outlaws. In 1883 Judge Isaac Parker convicted her and Sam of horse theft, and she served nine months in a Detroit prison. Sam was killed in 1886. On February 3, 1889, two days before her 41st birthday, she was shot from ambush while riding home. The killer was never identified. A dime novel published that year turned her into 'the Bandit Queen.'

ben-kilpatrick.bio: Ben Kilpatrick was born in Coleman County, Texas, and, being over six feet tall, became known as 'The Tall Texan.' He rode with the Black Jack Ketchum gang and then the Wild Bunch, took part in the Great Northern train robbery in Montana in 1901, and posed for the 'Fort Worth Five' photograph. He was arrested in St. Louis in 1901 and served about ten years in federal prison. Soon after his release, on March 13, 1912, he and an accomplice tried to rob a train near Sanderson, Texas. Express messenger David Trousdale clubbed him to death with an ice mallet.

ben-thompson.bio:
Ben Thompson was born in Knottingley, England, and came to Austin, Texas, as a boy. He fought for the Confederacy and then claimed to have served in Emperor Maximilian's army in Mexico. A skilled gambler and one of the most feared pistol shots of his day, he partnered with Phil Coe in the Bull's Head Saloon in Abilene in 1871 and clashed with Marshal Wild Bill Hickok. In Ellsworth in 1873 his brother Billy killed Sheriff Chauncey Whitney during a confrontation Ben was involved in.

In 1880 Austin elected him city marshal, and crime in the city dropped. In 1882 he killed San Antonio theater owner Jack Harris at the Vaudeville Theater and was acquitted. On March 11, 1884, he returned to the Vaudeville with his friend King Fisher, and both were killed in an ambush by Harris's friends, Thompson hit by nine bullets. He is buried in Austin's Oakwood Cemetery.

big-nose-kate.bio:
Mária Katalin Horony was born in Pest, Hungary, to a well-educated family that came to America and settled in Davenport, Iowa. Both of her parents died within a month of each other in 1865. She ran away from her foster home as a teenager and turned up as a dance hall girl and prostitute in St. Louis and then Kansas, including in Wichita at the same time the Earp family was there.

She met Doc Holliday at Fort Griffin, Texas, around 1877 and stayed with him, on and off, through Dodge City, Las Vegas, New Mexico, and Tombstone. Their relationship was famously stormy. In 1881, after a drunken fight, she signed an affidavit naming Doc as a suspect in a stagecoach robbery and killing near Benson, then took it back when she sobered up. They parted soon after.

She later married a blacksmith named George Cummings, separated from him, and lived quietly working as a housekeeper in Arizona. In 1931 she moved into the Arizona Pioneers' Home in Prescott, where she wrote letters about her years with Doc that historians still mine. She died there in 1940, just short of her 90th birthday.

bill-doolin.bio:
William Doolin was born in Arkansas and worked as a cowboy in Oklahoma, where he rode with the Dalton Gang. A lame horse kept him out of the Coffeyville raid in 1892, which may have saved his life. Afterward he formed his own gang, the 'Oklahombres' or Wild Bunch of Oklahoma, which robbed banks and trains across Oklahoma and Kansas.

In September 1893, deputy marshals surrounded the gang at Ingalls, Oklahoma Territory, and three lawmen were killed in the shootout. Bill Tilghman captured Doolin without a shot in a bathhouse in Eureka Springs, Arkansas, in January 1896, but he escaped from the Guthrie jail that July. On August 24, 1896, Heck Thomas's posse ambushed him near Lawson, Oklahoma, and killed him with a shotgun.

bill-longley.bio: William Preston Longley grew up in Texas during Reconstruction and began killing as a teenager, mostly freedmen and Union soldiers, which won him admirers among bitter ex-Confederates. He drifted across the West as a gambler and fugitive and claimed to have killed 32 men, though the real count is probably lower. He was arrested in Louisiana in 1877 and convicted of killing his childhood friend Wilson Anderson, whom he blamed for a relative's death. He was hanged in Giddings on October 11, 1878. A rumor that he survived the hanging and escaped circulated for decades, but a DNA test on his remains in 2001 confirmed he was the man in the grave.

bill-tilghman.bio:
William Matthew Tilghman Jr. was born at Fort Dodge, Iowa, and grew up in Kansas. He hunted buffalo and then became a lawman in Dodge City, serving as deputy and then city marshal. He moved to Oklahoma Territory in the 1889 land run and became a deputy U.S. marshal and one of the 'Three Guardsmen' with Heck Thomas and Chris Madsen. In January 1896 he captured Bill Doolin alone and without a shot in a bathhouse in Eureka Springs, Arkansas.

He served as an Oklahoma state senator and as police chief of Oklahoma City, and he produced a film about the outlaws he had chased, 'The Passing of the Oklahoma Outlaws' (1915). At 70 he took a job as marshal of the oil boomtown of Cromwell. On November 1, 1924, he tried to disarm a drunken Prohibition agent, Wiley Lynn, who shot him dead.

billy-claiborne.bio:
William Floyd Claiborne was born in Mississippi and came to Arizona as a cowboy, falling in with the Clantons and McLaurys. He liked to be called 'Billy the Kid' and is said to have killed several men. He was at the O.K. Corral on October 26, 1881, but ran from the fight into Fly's boarding house when the shooting began.

A year later, on November 14, 1882, a drunken Claiborne confronted bartender Buckskin Frank Leslie outside the Oriental Saloon in Tombstone, apparently believing Leslie had killed his friend Johnny Ringo. Leslie shot him dead. He is buried in Tombstone's Boothill.

billy-clanton.bio:
William Harrison Clanton was the youngest son of Newman 'Old Man' Clanton, born in Texas and raised on the family's ranches in Arizona. He worked cattle with his family and the McLaury brothers and was only 19 when he rode into Tombstone on October 26, 1881. Unlike his brother Ike, he had a gun in his hand when the shooting started.

Billy was hit in the wrist, chest and stomach at the O.K. Corral. Even down, he kept firing until his pistol was empty. He died soon after, asking for more cartridges. His father had been killed in the Guadalupe Canyon ambush that August. He is buried in Tombstone's Boothill next to the McLaurys under a marker that reads 'Murdered on the streets of Tombstone.'

billy-daniels.bio: William 'Billy' Daniels was a Cochise County deputy sheriff stationed in Bisbee. During the robbery of December 8, 1883, he opened fire on the robbers as they rode out of town. He led the pursuit and grew suspicious of John Heath, who kept pointing the posse in the wrong direction. He then followed the trail into Mexico and brought back Dan Dowd and Billy Delaney, and his testimony helped convict Heath.

billy-delaney.bio: William E. Delaney was one of the five Bisbee raiders. After the robbery he fled into Mexico, where he was captured at Minas Prietas, Sonora, and turned over to Arizona lawmen. He was convicted of murder in Tombstone and hanged on March 28, 1884. He is buried in Tombstone's Boothill.

bob-dalton.bio: Robert Reddick Dalton was born in Missouri and grew up in Kansas and Indian Territory, a cousin of the Younger brothers. Like his brothers Frank, Grat and Emmett, he started on the side of the law as a deputy U.S. marshal, but turned to horse theft. In 1890 he formed the Dalton Gang, which robbed trains in Indian Territory. Wanting to outdo the James-Younger Gang, he planned to rob two banks at once in Coffeyville, Kansas, on October 5, 1892. The townspeople recognized them, armed themselves and opened fire. Bob was killed in Death Alley along with Grat and two other gang members. He was 23.

bob-younger.bio: Robert Ewing Younger was the youngest Younger brother and was only about 22 at the time of the Northfield raid in 1876. His elbow was shattered in the gunfight, and his horse was killed as the gang fled. Cole and Jim stayed with him rather than leave him behind, which led to the brothers' capture near Madelia. He was sentenced to life at Stillwater Prison and died there of tuberculosis in 1889, at 35.

catfish-kid.bio: John Gough, known as the Catfish Kid, was a Tascosa tough connected with 'the System' faction. During the Big Fight on March 21, 1886, he fired from behind a woodpile and is believed to have killed Fred Chilton. At one point he pretended to be mortally wounded and then ran off unhurt when left alone. He was later convicted of killing an unarmed man in Tascosa and reportedly died in prison around 1890.

charles-goodnight.bio:
Charles Goodnight was born in Macoupin County, Illinois, and came to Texas in 1846 at age ten, riding bareback much of the way. He grew up in the Brazos River country working as a farmhand, freighter and cowboy, and served as a Texas Ranger and scout during the Comanche wars and the Civil War. He was a scout on the 1860 Pease River raid in which Cynthia Ann Parker was recaptured.

In 1866 he and Oliver Loving drove about 2,000 Longhorns west to Fort Sumner, New Mexico, blazing the Goodnight-Loving Trail. For that drive he rebuilt a surplus Army wagon into the first chuckwagon. When Loving died after a Comanche attack in 1867, Goodnight kept his promise and hauled his body hundreds of miles home to Texas, a story Larry McMurtry turned into 'Lonesome Dove.'

After losing money in Colorado in the Panic of 1873, he moved his herd into Palo Duro Canyon in 1876 and, with Irish investor John Adair, built the JA Ranch, which grew to nearly a million acres. He made peace with Comanche leader Quanah Parker, organized the Panhandle's first stockmen's association and, with his wife Molly, saved a herd of bison that helped keep the southern plains buffalo from extinction. He left the JA around 1888, ranched on his own at Goodnight, Texas, and lived to 93.

charley-emory.bio: Charles August Arnim, known in Tascosa as Charley Emory or 'Squirrel-Eye Charley,' was one of the Emory brothers in the 'System' faction and was related to Sally Emory, whose love life helped spark the trouble. He was shot in the leg during the Big Fight on March 21, 1886. He survived and lived until 1897.

charley-ford.bio: Charles Wilson Ford, Bob Ford's older brother, rode with Jesse James in the Blue Cut train robbery in 1881 and was in the room when Bob shot Jesse in April 1882. Both brothers were sentenced to hang and then pardoned the same day. He toured with Bob reenacting the killing, but he suffered from tuberculosis, guilt and a morphine habit, and on May 6, 1884, he shot himself near Richmond, Missouri.

charlie-bowdrie.bio: Charlie Bowdre was born in Georgia and raised in Mississippi before coming to New Mexico, where he and Doc Scurlock ran a ranch on the Ruidoso. He became one of the Regulators after John Tunstall's murder and is generally credited with firing the shot that mortally wounded Buckshot Roberts at Blazer's Mill. He also fought in the Battle of Lincoln. He married Manuela Herrera and stayed close to Billy the Kid. On December 23, 1880, at Stinking Springs, Pat Garrett's posse shot him as he stepped out of the rock house wearing a hat they mistook for the Kid's. He is buried at Fort Sumner in the same grave plot as the Kid and Tom O'Folliard.

cherokee-bill.bio: Crawford Goldsby was born at Fort Concho, Texas, to a Buffalo Soldier father and a mother of Cherokee, African American and white descent. He grew up in Indian Territory and Fort Gibson and was in trouble from his teens. In 1894 he joined the Cook Gang and went on a crime spree, killing several people, including Ernest Melton, an innocent bystander in a store robbery in Lenapah. He was captured in 1895. While awaiting execution in the Fort Smith jail he obtained a gun and killed guard Lawrence Keating during an escape attempt. He was hanged on March 17, 1896, at age 20. His last words are said to have been, 'I came here to die, not to make a speech.'

chris-madsen.bio: Christian Madsen was born in Denmark and served in the Danish army before coming to America in 1876. His claim of service in the French Foreign Legion has been questioned. He spent 15 years in the U.S. 5th Cavalry, fighting in the Indian Wars, and then became a deputy U.S. marshal in Oklahoma Territory. As one of the 'Three Guardsmen' with Heck Thomas and Bill Tilghman, he helped break up the Doolin gang; his posses killed Doolin gang members Dynamite Dan Clifton and Little Dick West. He served as a Rough Rider in the Spanish-American War and later as Oklahoma City police chief. He died in Guthrie in 1944, the last of the three.

chuck-colbert.bio: Chunk Colbert was a Texas-born gunman said to have killed several men. On January 7, 1874, he and Clay Allison raced horses near the Clifton House stage station in Colfax County, New Mexico, and then sat down to dinner together. According to the most common version, Colbert reached for his pistol under the table, the barrel caught on the table edge, and Allison shot him in the head. Asked why he had sat down to eat with a man who wanted to kill him, Allison is said to have replied that he didn't want to send a man to hell on an empty stomach.

cole-younger.bio:
Thomas Coleman Younger was born near Lee's Summit, Missouri, to a prosperous family. In 1862 Union militiamen murdered his father, and Cole joined William Quantrill's guerrillas, taking part in the raid on Lawrence, Kansas. After the war he and three of his brothers joined Frank and Jesse James in the James-Younger Gang.

At Northfield, Minnesota, on September 7, 1876, the townspeople fought back. Two gang members were killed in the street, and Cole and his brothers Jim and Bob were captured two weeks later near Madelia after a running manhunt, Cole carrying about 11 wounds. They pleaded guilty to avoid hanging and were sentenced to life at Stillwater Prison, where Cole became a model prisoner.

He was paroled in 1901 and pardoned in 1903, on condition he never return to Minnesota. He toured with Frank James in a Wild West show and gave a lecture titled 'What My Life Has Taught Me,' warning young people against crime. He died at Lee's Summit in 1916 with, it was said, 17 bullets still in his body.

commodore-perry-owens.bio: Commodore Perry Owens was born in Tennessee and named for the naval hero of Lake Erie. He went west as a cowboy and buffalo hunter and became known in Arizona for his long hair and skill with a rifle. In 1886 he was elected sheriff of Apache County during the Pleasant Valley War. On September 4, 1887, he went to the Blevins house in Holbrook to arrest Andy Blevins (also called Andy Cooper) for horse theft. In about a minute of shooting he killed three men and wounded a fourth with his Winchester, without being hit. He later became the first sheriff of Navajo County and lived out his life as a businessman in Seligman, Arizona.

d-tom-smith.bio: D. Tom Smith was a Cochise County deputy sheriff who happened to be eating dinner at the Bisbee House on December 8, 1883. When the shooting started outside, he ran into the street and told the gunmen he was an officer. They shot him dead. He was one of the victims of the Bisbee Massacre.

dallas-stoudenmire.bio: Dallas Stoudenmire was born in Alabama and fought for the Confederacy as a teenager, being wounded several times. Tall and imposing, he served in the Texas Rangers and became El Paso's city marshal in April 1881. Three days later he took part in the 'Four Dead in Five Seconds' gunfight, killing three men in the street. He tamed the town but drank heavily and feuded with the powerful Manning brothers. Forced to resign in 1882, he later became a deputy U.S. marshal. On September 18, 1882, a confrontation with the Mannings in a saloon ended with him shot dead. He is buried in Alleyton, Texas.

dan-dowd.bio: Daniel 'Big Dan' Dowd was one of the five gunmen in the Bisbee robbery of December 8, 1883. He stood guard on the street outside the Goldwater & Castañeda store and fired on townspeople who came to see what was happening. He fled to Mexico, where Deputy Billy Daniels tracked him down and brought him back. He was tried in Tombstone, convicted of murder, and hanged with the other four on March 28, 1884. He is buried in Tombstone's Boothill.

dan-dowd.notes: Stood guard outside the store and shot at townspeople.

dave-mather.bio: David Allen Mather was born in Connecticut and claimed descent from the Puritan minister Cotton Mather. He was a quiet man, which may be where 'Mysterious Dave' came from. He drifted through Dodge City, Las Vegas, New Mexico, where he was a policeman and member of the Dodge City Gang, and Texas as a gambler, rustler and sometime lawman. In 1879 he rode with Bat Masterson in the Royal Gorge War. Back in Dodge City as assistant marshal, he was involved in a feud with Tom Nixon, who shot at him, and on July 21, 1884, Mather killed Nixon. He was acquitted. After 1887 he vanished; reports had him in Canada and elsewhere, but his fate is unknown.

legends.text: Vanished without a trace

dave-mather.name: Dave Mather

dave-rudabaugh.bio:
David Rudabaugh was born in Illinois and grew up in Kansas, where he started out as a rustler and train robber. Wyatt Earp chased him all the way to Fort Griffin, Texas, in 1877; Bat Masterson captured him in 1878, and he informed on his partners to avoid prison. He then went to Las Vegas, New Mexico, where he joined the corrupt 'Dodge City Gang' of police and gamblers and killed a jailer during a breakout.

He rode with Billy the Kid and was captured with him at Stinking Springs in 1880. He escaped from the Las Vegas jail in 1881 and fled to Mexico. In Parral, Chihuahua, on February 18, 1886, he killed men in a cantina fight over cards, and townspeople then killed and beheaded him and paraded his head on a pole. He got the nickname 'Dirty Dave' because he was said to rarely bathe.

legends.text: Head paraded on a pole

dave-rudabaugh.name: Dave Rudabaugh

sources.title: Book: James B. Mills, Billy the Kid: El Bandido Simpático (2022)

davis-tutt.bio: Davis Kasey Tutt was born in Arkansas, and his family was caught up in the violent Tutt–Everett feud there. He served in the Confederate Army and then settled in Springfield, Missouri, as a gambler. He and Wild Bill Hickok had been friends but fell out, possibly over a woman. In July 1865 Tutt took Hickok's gold pocket watch as security for a gambling debt and said he would wear it across the town square. On July 21, 1865, the two faced each other on the square and fired at about the same time. Tutt missed. Hickok's bullet struck him in the chest, killing him. Hickok was tried for manslaughter and acquitted. Tutt's half-brother Lewis later moved him to Maple Park Cemetery.

legends.text: Took Hickok's gold pocket watch as security for a gambling debt
He and Hickok fell out over a woman

davis-tutt.name: Davis Kasey Tutt
davis-tutt.notes: Birth year varies: Wikipedia gives c. 1836, his gravestone says 1839. First buried in Springfield's old city cemetery; his half-brother Lewis Tutt moved him to Maple Park in March 1883. His headstone shows a pocket watch, playing cards and pistols.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Davis Tutt
Springfield-Greene County Library: Lewis and Davis Tutt
Legends of America: Hickok–Tutt Gunfight
Book: Tom Clavin, Wild Bill: The True Story of the American Frontier's First Gunfighter (2019)

ed-king.bio: Ed King was a former Texas Ranger who worked as a cowboy for the LS Ranch in the Texas Panhandle. He was involved with Sally Emory, the former girlfriend of bartender Lem Woodruff, and reportedly taunted Woodruff in the days before the fight. Early on March 21, 1886, outside the Jenkins Saloon in Tascosa, Woodruff shot King in the face, killing him and starting the Big Fight. He was buried in Tascosa's Boot Hill.
incidents: Big Fight at the Jenkins Saloon (1886)

legends.text: Taunted Lem Woodruff as 'Pretty Lem' in the days before the fight

ed-king.name: Ed King

sources.title: Wikipedia: Big Fight at the Jenkins Saloon
True West: The Big Fight

ed-masterson.bio: Edward John Masterson was Bat's older brother, a friendly, easygoing man who served as an assistant and then city marshal of Dodge City. Some thought he was too trusting for the job. On April 9, 1878, he tried to disarm a drunken cowboy named Jack Wagner outside the Lady Gay Saloon. Wagner's pistol went off at point-blank range and set Ed's coat on fire. Ed shot back, mortally wounding Wagner and his trail boss, Alf Walker, then walked across the street and collapsed. He died within the hour. Bat, who was nearby, is sometimes credited with the shots that hit Wagner and Walker, though accounts differ.
incidents: Killed on duty as Dodge City Marshal
ed-masterson.name: Ed Masterson
ed-masterson.resting: Maple Grove Cemetery — Dodge City, KS

sources.title: Book: Tom Clavin, Dodge City: Wyatt Earp, Bat Masterson, and the Wickedest Town in the American West (2017)

elfego-baca.bio: Elfego Baca was born in Socorro, New Mexico, and raised partly in Kansas. In 1884, at 19, he appointed himself a deputy and arrested a drunken cowboy in Frisco (now Reserve), New Mexico, for shooting up the town. Dozens of the cowboy's friends from the nearby ranches came after him. He holed up in a small jacal and held them off for some 33 hours while they fired, reportedly, thousands of rounds into it. He killed four of his attackers and walked away nearly unhurt. He was tried for murder twice and acquitted both times. Baca went on to become a lawyer, county sheriff, district attorney and politician, and he lived until 1945. Disney made him the subject of a 1950s TV series.

legends.text: Survived some 4,000 bullets fired at his hut

elfego-baca.name: Elfego Baca

elzy-lay.bio: William Ellsworth 'Elzy' Lay was born in Ohio and grew up in Colorado. He became Butch Cassidy's closest friend and right-hand man, and is considered the planner behind the Castle Gate payroll robbery in 1897. In 1899 he took part in the Black Jack Ketchum gang's train robbery near Folsom, New Mexico, and was wounded and captured after a shootout in which Sheriff Edward Farr was killed. Sentenced to life, he was pardoned in 1906. He married, worked as a ranch manager and oil geologist and helped design irrigation projects in California. He died in Los Angeles in 1934.
elzy-lay.name: William Ellsworth Lay
elzy-lay.resting: Forest Lawn Memorial Park — Glendale, CA

sources.title: Wikipedia: Elzy Lay

emmett-dalton.bio:
Emmett Dalton was the youngest member of the Dalton Gang and was only 21 at Coffeyville in 1892. He was the only one of the five raiders to survive, shot about 23 times, including while trying to help his dying brother Bob. He was sentenced to life in the Kansas penitentiary and pardoned in 1907 after 14 years.

He married his old sweetheart, Julia Johnson, and moved to California, where he became a real estate agent and building contractor, wrote a book called 'When the Daltons Rode' and worked on Westerns in Hollywood. He spoke out against crime for the rest of his life and died in Los Angeles in 1937.

legends.text: Later a Hollywood writer

emmett-dalton.name: Emmett Dalton

sources.title: Book: James Reasoner, Draw: The Greatest Gunfights of the American West (2003)

etta-place.bio: Etta Place is the great mystery of the Wild Bunch. She was the Sundance Kid's companion, and her real name, birthplace and fate are all unknown; even 'Etta Place' may be an alias. She posed for a portrait with Sundance in New York in 1901 before sailing with him and Butch Cassidy to Argentina, where they ranched in Cholila. She returned to the U.S. around 1906, and after that she disappears from the record. Theories have tied her to a schoolteacher, a Fort Worth prostitute and several women who lived into the 20th century, but none has been proven.
incidents: Sailed to Argentina with Butch and Sundance (1901)

legends.text: Her real name and fate are unknown

etta-place.name: Etta Place

frank-coe.bio: Frank Coe was a cousin of George Coe and a rancher on the Ruidoso who sided with the Tunstall–McSween faction in the Lincoln County War. He rode with the Regulators at Blazer's Mill and survived a shootout at the Fritz Ranch in April 1878 in which Frank McNab was killed and Coe was captured. He later escaped. After the war he settled down as a farmer and rancher in the Ruidoso Valley and lived into the 1930s, sharing his memories with historians.
frank-coe.name: Frank Coe
frank-coe.notes: Place of death and burial site are not confirmed.

sources.title: SNAC: Frank Coe
Book: James B. Mills, Billy the Kid: El Bandido Simpático (2022)

frank-dalton.bio: Frank Dalton was the oldest of the Dalton brothers who rode for the law and the only one who stayed on that side of it. He served as a deputy U.S. marshal under Judge Isaac Parker's court at Fort Smith. On November 27, 1887, he was killed in a shootout with whiskey smugglers and horse thieves along the Arkansas River in Indian Territory. His death is often cited as one reason his younger brothers, who had briefly served as lawmen themselves, turned to crime.
incidents: Killed on duty as Deputy U.S. Marshal
frank-dalton.name: Frank Dalton

frank-james.bio:
Alexander Franklin James was born in Missouri and was the older, quieter and more bookish of the James brothers; he liked to quote Shakespeare. He fought for the Confederacy at Wilson's Creek and then rode with William Quantrill's guerrillas, including the raid on Lawrence, Kansas, in 1863. After the war he robbed banks and trains alongside Jesse and the Younger brothers and escaped the Northfield disaster in 1876.

Six months after Jesse's murder, in October 1882, Frank walked into Governor Thomas Crittenden's office and handed over his pistol. He was tried for murder in Missouri and robbery in Alabama and acquitted both times. He spent the rest of his life in a string of ordinary jobs: shoe salesman, racetrack betting commissioner, theater doorman. In 1903 he toured in a Wild West show with Cole Younger. In his final years he gave tours of the family farm in Kearney for a fee, and he died there in 1915.
frank-james.name: Frank James

frank-leslie.bio:
Nashville Franklin 'Buckskin Frank' Leslie claimed to have been an army scout and much else; few of his stories can be verified. In Tombstone he tended bar at the Oriental Saloon. In 1880 he shot and killed Mike Killeen, then married Killeen's widow, May. In November 1882 he killed Billy Claiborne in a street confrontation outside the Oriental.

In 1889, at a ranch in the Swisshelm Mountains, he shot and killed his companion, Blonde Mollie Williams, and wounded a ranch hand. Sheriff John Slaughter took him to the Yuma Territorial Prison, where he served about seven years. After his release he drifted to Mexico, Alaska and California, worked in a San Francisco pool hall, and disappeared from the record after the early 1920s.

legends.text: Disappeared after 1922

frank-leslie.name: Frank Leslie

sources.title: Wikipedia: Buckskin Frank Leslie

frank-mclaury.bio:
Robert Findley 'Frank' McLaury was born in Kortright, New York, and came west with his brother Tom after time in Iowa and Texas. By 1880 the brothers had a ranch near the Babocomari River and later in Sulphur Springs Valley, and were accused of dealing in stolen Army mules and rustled Mexican cattle. Frank was proud and quick to take offense, and he took Virgil Earp's search for stolen mules as a personal insult.

At the O.K. Corral he was considered the most dangerous of the Cowboys. He was shot in the stomach early in the fight, but staggered into the street with his horse as cover and kept firing, hitting Morgan Earp, before a bullet to the head finished him. Brother Will McLaury, a Texas lawyer, came to Tombstone to prosecute the Earps and is suspected of later financing revenge.
frank-mclaury.name: Frank McLaury

sources.title: Book: Tom Clavin, Tombstone: The Earp Brothers, Doc Holliday, and the Vendetta Ride from Hell (2020)

frank-stillwell.bio:
Frank C. Stilwell was born in Iowa, the younger brother of famed scout Jack Stilwell. In Arizona he ran a saloon, worked in mining and freighting and served as a deputy under Sheriff Johnny Behan, while running with the Cowboy faction. He and Pete Spence were arrested for the Bisbee stagecoach robbery in 1881.

He was named as a suspect in the murder of Morgan Earp. Two days later, on March 20, 1882, he was found near the Tucson train yard, where the Earps were escorting Virgil's family onto a westbound train. His body was riddled with buckshot and bullets. Wyatt Earp was indicted for the killing, and the Vendetta Ride began that night.
frank-stillwell.name: Frank Stilwell

sources.title: Wikipedia: Frank Stilwell
Book: Tom Clavin, Tombstone: The Earp Brothers, Doc Holliday, and the Vendetta Ride from Hell (2020)

frank-valley.bio: Frank Valley (or Vallé) was an LS Ranch cowboy and friend of Ed King. After King was shot outside the Jenkins Saloon in Tascosa on March 21, 1886, Valley and the others went after Lem Woodruff, and Valley wounded him. Valley then opened a door at the back of the saloon and was shot in the head and killed. He is buried in Tascosa's Boot Hill.
incidents: Big Fight at the Jenkins Saloon (1886)
frank-valley.name: Frank Valley
frank-valley.notes: Boot Hill grave No. 4. Shot in the head as he opened a door behind the saloon.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Big Fight at the Jenkins Saloon
True West: The Big Fight

fred-chilton.bio: Fred Chilton was another LS Ranch cowboy who joined in the Big Fight in Tascosa on March 21, 1886. In the dark and confusion he shot and killed restaurant owner Jesse Sheets, apparently mistaking him for Louis Bousman. Moments later he was shot himself, probably by the Catfish Kid firing from a woodpile. As he died he handed his gun to John Lang. He is buried in Tascosa's Boot Hill.
incidents: Big Fight at the Jenkins Saloon (1886)

legends.text: Handed his gun to John Lang as he died

fred-chilton.name: Fred Chilton

sources.title: Wikipedia: Big Fight at the Jenkins Saloon
True West: The Big Fight

george-coe.bio: George Washington Coe was born in Iowa and followed his cousin Frank to New Mexico's Ruidoso Valley to farm. He joined the Regulators after Tunstall's murder. At Blazer's Mill, Buckshot Roberts shot off his trigger finger. He fought in the Battle of Lincoln and then left the territory for a time. He returned to farm near Glencoe and lived to 1941, one of the last surviving Regulators. His memoir, 'Frontier Fighter' (1934), is an important firsthand account of Billy the Kid.

legends.text: Wrote memoir 'Frontier Fighter'

george-coe.name: George Coe

sources.title: Wikipedia: George W. Coe
Book: James B. Mills, Billy the Kid: El Bandido Simpático (2022)

gratton-dalton.bio: Gratton 'Grat' Dalton was a deputy U.S. marshal before he turned outlaw, and he was arrested in California for a train robbery there in 1891 and escaped. He rode with his brothers in the Dalton Gang's Indian Territory train robberies. At Coffeyville on October 5, 1892, he led the group robbing the Condon Bank, where a clerk stalled him by claiming the vault had a time lock. By the time they came out, the town was armed. Grat was shot dead in Death Alley, reportedly by livery stable owner John Kloehr.
gratton-dalton.name: Gratton Dalton

sources.title: Book: James Reasoner, Draw: The Greatest Gunfights of the American West (2003)

harry-longabaugh.bio:
Harry Alonzo Longabaugh was born in Mont Clare, Pennsylvania, and went west at 15. In 1887, in Sundance, Wyoming, he stole a horse, saddle and gun and served 18 months in the town jail, which gave him his nickname. He worked as a cowboy and was part of a bank robbery in Montana in the 1890s before joining Butch Cassidy's Wild Bunch.

He was considered the best shot in the gang. In 1900 he sat for the famous 'Fort Worth Five' photograph with Butch, Kid Curry, Ben Kilpatrick and Will Carver. In 1901 he sailed for Argentina with Butch and Etta Place, and in November 1908 he died with Butch at San Vicente, Bolivia. The 1969 film 'Butch Cassidy and the Sundance Kid' made him a household name.
harry-longabaugh.dateNote: Death usually given as Nov 7, 1908; some accounts say Nov 3 or 6.

legends.text: Rumors of Survival

harry-longabaugh.name: Harry Longabaugh

sources.title: Book: Bryan Burrough, The Gunfighters: How Texas Made the West Wild (2025)

harvey-logan.bio:
Harvey Alexander Logan was born in Iowa and grew up with an aunt in Dodson, Missouri, along with his brothers. They went to Montana as cowboys and took the last name Curry from an outlaw they admired. In 1894 Harvey killed rancher Pike Landusky in a saloon fight in Landusky, Montana, and fled. He joined the Wild Bunch and became its most violent member, killing several lawmen, including two sheriffs who chased the gang after the Wilcox train robbery in 1899.

Captured in Knoxville, Tennessee, in 1901 after shooting two policemen, he escaped from the jail in 1903. In June 1904, after a train robbery near Parachute, Colorado, he was wounded by a posse and shot himself rather than be captured. He is buried in Glenwood Springs, near Doc Holliday's memorial.

legends.text: Rumors of Survival

harvey-logan.name: Harvey Logan
harvey-logan.notes: Some sources give Richland Township, Tama County, IA.

sources.title: Legends of America: Kid Curry

heck-thomas.bio:
Henry Andrew 'Heck' Thomas was born in Oxford, Georgia, and as a boy served as a courier for his uncle's Confederate regiment. He moved to Texas and in 1878 was an express guard on a train robbed by Sam Bass's gang, where he hid most of the money in a stove. He went on to become a deputy U.S. marshal for Judge Isaac Parker's court and spent decades hunting outlaws in Indian Territory, including Ned Christie.

With Bill Tilghman and Chris Madsen he became one of Oklahoma's 'Three Guardsmen,' who are credited with breaking up the outlaw gangs of the 1890s. On August 24, 1896, his posse killed Bill Doolin near Lawson, Oklahoma. He later served as the first police chief of Lawton and died there in 1912.
heck-thomas.dateNote: Some sources give his birth as Jan 3, 1850 and his death as Aug 15, 1912.

legends.text: One of the 'Three Guardsmen'
Wounded more than six times in the line of duty

heck-thomas.name: Henry Andrew Thomas

sources.title: Wikipedia: Heck Thomas
Encyclopedia of Oklahoma History: Heck Thomas

henry-starr.bio:
Henry Starr was born near Fort Gibson in the Cherokee Nation. He was part Cherokee and a nephew of Sam Starr, which made Belle Starr his aunt by marriage. He began robbing banks and stores in the early 1890s and killed Deputy Marshal Floyd Wilson in 1892. Judge Isaac Parker sentenced him to hang twice, but both convictions were overturned, and in prison he helped talk Cherokee Bill into giving up his gun during an escape attempt.

Pardoned by President Theodore Roosevelt in 1903, he went back to robbing banks, and he is often said to have robbed more banks than anyone else in America. In March 1915 his gang tried to rob two banks at once in Stroud, Oklahoma, and a teenage boy shot him with a rifle. After another prison term he starred in a silent film about his own life, 'A Debtor to the Law' (1919). On February 18, 1921, he was shot during a bank robbery in Harrison, Arkansas, and died four days later. He was one of the first bank robbers to use a car for a getaway.
incidents: Starred in 'A Debtor to the Law' (1919)

legends.text: Robbed more banks than any man in America
First bank robber to use a getaway car

henry-starr.name: Henry Starr

sources.title: Wikipedia: Henry Starr
Encyclopedia of Oklahoma History: Henry Starr

ike-clanton.bio:
Joseph Isaac Clanton was born in Callaway County, Missouri, the son of Newman 'Old Man' Clanton, whose ranch near Tombstone was a gathering place for the Cowboys and a market for rustled Mexican cattle. Ike was a loudmouth with a drinking problem who spent much of the night before the O.K. Corral threatening to kill the Earps and Doc Holliday.

When the shooting started on October 26, 1881, Ike was unarmed. He grabbed Wyatt's arm, was told to fight or get away, and ran into Fly's Photo Gallery, leaving his brother Billy and the McLaurys to die. He then filed murder charges against the Earps and Holliday, which Justice Wells Spicer dismissed. He was suspected in the ambush of Virgil and the murder of Morgan but never convicted.

Ike kept rustling cattle in Arizona for years. On June 1, 1887, detective Jonas Brighton tracked him to a ranch at Eagle Creek and shot him dead when, according to Brighton, Ike reached for his rifle.
ike-clanton.name: Ike Clanton
ike-clanton.notes: Grave site near Springerville, AZ is approximate.

sources.title: Book: Tom Clavin, Tombstone: The Earp Brothers, Doc Holliday, and the Vendetta Ride from Hell (2020)

isaac-parker.bio:
Isaac Charles Parker was born in Barnesville, Ohio, became a lawyer in St. Joseph, Missouri, and served two terms in Congress. In 1875, at 36, President Grant appointed him judge of the federal court for the Western District of Arkansas at Fort Smith, which also covered Indian Territory, a refuge for outlaws.

Over 21 years his court heard more than 13,000 cases. He sentenced 160 people to death, and 79 were hanged, giving him the nickname 'The Hanging Judge,' though he personally opposed the death penalty and favored rehabilitation. His roughly 200 deputy marshals, including Bass Reeves and Heck Thomas, covered 74,000 square miles, and many of them were killed doing it. In 1896 Congress took Indian Territory away from his court. He died that November.
incidents: Federal judge for the Western District of Arkansas (1875–1896)

legends.text: Sentenced 160 people to death; 79 were hanged

isaac-parker.name: Isaac Charles Parker
isaac-parker.resting: Fort Smith National Cemetery — Fort Smith, AR

sources.title: NPS: Heck Thomas

jack-johnson.bio: John 'Turkey Creek Jack' Johnson is a shadowy figure; he may have been born John Blount in Missouri. He was in Deadwood in 1876, where he reportedly survived a duel in which he killed two men, and later turned up in Tombstone as a friend of Wyatt Earp. He rode on the Vendetta Ride in 1882 and fled Arizona with the posse. Researchers have tied him to John Blount, who died of tuberculosis in Salt Lake City in 1887.

legends.text: Real name possibly John Blount

jack-johnson.name: Jack Johnson

sources.title: Wikipedia: Jack Johnson
Legends of America: Turkey Creek Jack Johnson

jack-mccall.bio: John 'Jack' McCall was a drifter and buffalo hunter from Kentucky. On August 2, 1876, he walked into Saloon No. 10 in Deadwood and shot Wild Bill Hickok in the back of the head. One theory says he was angry over losing at poker to Hickok the day before. A miners' court in Deadwood, which had no legal standing, acquitted him after he claimed Hickok had killed his brother. He was rearrested in Wyoming. Because the first trial had no legal authority, he could be tried again. A federal court in Yankton, Dakota Territory, convicted him, and he was hanged on March 1, 1877. It later came out that he had no brother.

legends.text: Buried with the noose on

jack-mccall.name: Jack McCall
jack-mccall.notes: The original cemetery was moved; the grave's location is lost.

sources.title: Book: Tom Clavin, Wild Bill: The True Story of the American Frontier's First Gunfighter (2019)

jack-vermillion.bio: John Wilson Vermillion was a Virginian who drifted west and ended up in Tombstone, where he became a friend of the Earps and rode with Wyatt on the Vendetta Ride in 1882. Why he was called 'Texas Jack' is unclear; one story says he gave Texas as his home to avoid questions. He was reportedly in the fight at Iron Springs where Curly Bill was killed. After Arizona he spent time gambling in Colorado, where he may have known Soapy Smith, before returning to Virginia, where he lived as a farmer until his death in 1911. He is not the same man as Texas Jack Omohundro.

legends.text: 'Texas Jack' because he was from Virginia

jack-vermillion.name: Jack Vermillion

sources.title: Wikipedia: Texas Jack Vermillion

james-butler-hickok.bio:
James Butler Hickok was born in Troy Grove, Illinois, where his family is said to have helped runaway slaves on the Underground Railroad. He went to Kansas as a teenager and worked as a stagecoach driver and freighter. In 1861, at Rock Creek Station in Nebraska, he killed David McCanles and two other men; it was later blown up into a legend of him killing ten men single-handedly. During the Civil War he served the Union as a wagon master, scout and spy.

On July 21, 1865, in the town square of Springfield, Missouri, he shot gambler Davis Tutt at about 75 yards in one of the first true quick-draw duels on record. A Harper's Monthly article in 1867 made 'Wild Bill' a national celebrity. He scouted for the Army, including Custer's 7th Cavalry, and served as sheriff of Ellis County at Hays City and as marshal of Abilene in 1871. In Abilene he shot gambler Phil Coe and, in the confusion, accidentally killed his own deputy, Mike Williams, which haunted him.

He toured briefly with Buffalo Bill on stage, married circus owner Agnes Lake in 1876 and went to the Black Hills hoping to make money. On August 2, 1876, while he played poker in Nuttal & Mann's Saloon No. 10 in Deadwood with his back to the door, Jack McCall shot him in the back of the head. His hand, reported as black aces and eights, became known as the Dead Man's Hand. He was 39.

legends.text: Dead Man's Hand (aces & eights)

james-butler-hickok.name: James Butler Hickok

sources.title: Book: Tom Clavin, Wild Bill: The True Story of the American Frontier's First Gunfighter (2019)

weapons: Pair of ivory-handled 1851 Colt Navy revolvers

james-dolan.bio:
James Joseph Dolan was born in Loughrea, Ireland, and came to the U.S. as a child. He served in the Union Army and came to Fort Stanton, New Mexico, where he went to work for Lawrence Murphy and became his partner in the House, the store that dominated Lincoln County's trade and government contracts. He was a short, aggressive man who once tried to shoot an Army officer.

When John Tunstall and Alexander McSween set up a rival store, Dolan fought back, first in the courts and then by hiring gunmen, including the Jesse Evans Gang and the Seven Rivers Warriors. He was indicted for Tunstall's murder and later in the killing of McSween's widow's lawyer, Huston Chapman, but was never convicted. When the war ended he took over Tunstall's store and ranch, served as county treasurer and in the territorial senate, and died on his ranch in 1898.
james-dolan.dateNote: Death date given as either February 6 or February 26, 1898.
incidents: Partner in L.G. Murphy & Co. ('The House')
Indicted for the murder of John Tunstall
Indicted in the Huston Chapman killing (Feb 1879)
Lincoln County Treasurer and Territorial Senator

james-dolan.name: James Joseph Dolan
james-dolan.notes: Came to the U.S. at age 5, served in the Union Army, and clerked for Murphy at Fort Stanton before becoming his partner. He hired the Jesse Evans Gang, the Seven Rivers Warriors and the John Kinney Gang. He was never convicted of anything; he later bought Tunstall's store and ranch and went into politics. The Murphy–Dolan store later became the Lincoln County Courthouse.

sources.title: Wikipedia: James Dolan
Legends of America: James Dolan

james-masterson.bio: James Patrick Masterson was the younger brother of Bat and Ed. He served as a Dodge City marshal, ran a dance hall there and was involved in a business dispute in 1881 that brought Bat back to town for the Plaza shootout. He later went to New Mexico, where he fought in the Colfax County troubles, and then to Oklahoma, where he became a deputy U.S. marshal and fought in the Battle of Ingalls against the Doolin gang in 1893. He died of tuberculosis in Guthrie in 1895.
james-masterson.dateNote: Born September 1855; sources disagree between the 16th and 18th.
james-masterson.name: James Masterson

sources.title: Book: Tom Clavin, Dodge City: Wyatt Earp, Bat Masterson, and the Wickedest Town in the American West (2017)

jc-tappenier.bio: J.C. Tappenier was an assayer in Bisbee. During the robbery of December 8, 1883, the gunmen outside the store ordered him back into the Bon Ton Saloon. When he refused, they shot him in the head. He was one of the victims of the Bisbee Massacre.
jc-tappenier.name: J. C. Tappenier
jc-tappenier.notes: An assayer, shot in the head after refusing to go back into the Bon Ton Saloon.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Bisbee massacre

jefferson-smith.bio:
Jefferson Randolph Smith II was born in Coweta County, Georgia, and grew up in Texas. In Denver in the 1880s he became famous for the 'prize soap' swindle: he wrapped bars of soap in bills of up to $100, sold them on the street for a few dollars, and made sure only his shills ever won. The trick gave him his nickname, and he grew into the boss of Denver's underworld, controlling gambling, bribing police and politicians, and running a gang of con men.

He moved his operations to the boomtown of Creede, Colorado, in 1892, then back to Denver, and in 1897 to Skagway, Alaska, gateway to the Klondike gold rush. There his Soap Gang ran fake businesses, including a telegraph office with no wires, to fleece prospectors. On July 8, 1898, after his men robbed a miner of his gold, Smith confronted vigilante guard Frank Reid on the Juneau Wharf. Both fired, and Smith was killed. Reid died of his wounds days later.

legends.text: Annual 'Soapy Smith Wake' in Skagway

jefferson-smith.name: Jefferson Smith

jesse-chisholm.bio:
Jesse Chisholm was born in Tennessee around 1805 to a Scottish father and a Cherokee mother, and came west to Arkansas and then Indian Territory as a young man with the Cherokee. He became one of the best-known traders and guides on the southern plains. He spoke many Native languages, and for some 20 years he interpreted and helped broker treaties between the Republic of Texas, the United States and the Plains tribes. He was known for buying captive children out of slavery and raising several of them himself.

During the Civil War he moved north into Kansas with refugee Wichita families and kept a trading post near the site of present-day Wichita. Around 1865 he hauled goods by wagon south from there to his trading posts on the North Canadian River, and the deep ruts he left became a road. When Texas cattle herds came north to Abilene beginning in 1867, drovers followed Chisholm's road across Indian Territory and soon gave his name to the whole route.

Chisholm never drove cattle and probably never heard of the trail that made him famous. He died at Left Hand Spring in March 1868, reportedly of food poisoning from bear meat cooked in a brass kettle, and was buried there.

jesse-james.bio:
Jesse Woodson James was born in Clay County, Missouri. His father, a Baptist preacher, went to the California gold fields and died there when Jesse was three. The James family owned slaves and sided with the South, and during the Civil War Jesse followed his older brother Frank into the Confederate guerrillas, riding with 'Bloody Bill' Anderson. He was in the band responsible for the Centralia massacre in 1864 and was badly wounded in the chest in 1865 while trying to surrender.

After the war Jesse and Frank teamed up with Cole Younger and his brothers to rob banks, starting with Liberty, Missouri, in 1866, and later trains, starting at Adair, Iowa, in 1873. Newspaper editor John Newman Edwards cast Jesse as a Confederate Robin Hood avenging the South, an image that made him a celebrity, though there is no evidence the gang ever shared the money. In January 1875 a Pinkerton raid on the family farm threw an incendiary device into the house; it killed Jesse's nine-year-old half-brother and cost his mother her arm, and public sympathy swung his way.

The gang was destroyed at Northfield, Minnesota, in September 1876. Jesse and Frank escaped, and Jesse lived for a while under the name J.D. Howard in Nashville before forming a new gang in 1879. Governor Thomas Crittenden posted a large reward. On April 3, 1882, at his home in St. Joseph, Missouri, Jesse got up on a chair to straighten or dust a picture, and new gang member Robert Ford shot him in the back of the head. He was 34. A DNA test on his exhumed remains in 1995 confirmed the body was his.

jesse-sheets.bio: Jesse Sheets owned a restaurant in Tascosa. When the shooting broke out early on March 21, 1886, he stepped outside to see what was happening. LS cowboy Fred Chilton, mistaking him in the dark for Louis Bousman, shot him dead. He was the innocent bystander of the Big Fight. He was first buried in Tascosa's Boot Hill, and in 1929 his family moved him to Roswell, New Mexico.

jim-coutright.bio: Timothy Isaiah 'Longhair Jim' Courtright was born in Illinois and served as a Union Army scout. He became the city marshal of Fort Worth in 1876 and was considered effective at taming its rough Hell's Half Acre district. After losing re-election he worked as a lawman and hired gun in New Mexico, where he was charged in the killing of two settlers, and fled. Back in Fort Worth he ran the T.I.C. Commercial Detective Agency, which collected protection money from gambling halls. When Luke Short refused to pay, Courtright confronted him outside the White Elephant Saloon on February 8, 1887. His revolver reportedly caught on his watch chain, and Short shot him dead.

jim-east.bio: James Henry East was born in Illinois and came to Texas as a cowboy. He rode with Pat Garrett's posse in 1880 and was at the capture of Billy the Kid at Stinking Springs. He worked for the LS Ranch in the Texas Panhandle and was elected sheriff of Oldham County, based in Tascosa, in 1882. After the Big Fight at the Jenkins Saloon in 1886 he restored order and helped bring charges. In 1889 he killed gambler Tom Clark. He moved to Douglas, Arizona, in 1903 and served as its city marshal and police chief. He later co-wrote a play about Billy the Kid.

jim-miller.bio:
James Brown Miller was born in Arkansas and raised in Texas. As a child he lost his family and was sent to live with his grandparents, who were murdered; he was suspected but never charged. He was a churchgoing man who did not drink or swear, which earned him the nickname 'Deacon Jim,' but he worked as a hired killer, usually with a shotgun from ambush, charging a set fee per killing.

He is believed to have killed his brother-in-law and later Sheriff Bud Frazer of Reeves County, and he is the leading suspect in the 1908 killing of Pat Garrett. In 1909 he was hired to kill rancher Gus Bobbitt near Ada, Oklahoma. He was caught, and on April 19, 1909, a mob dragged him and three men who had hired him from the jail and hanged them in a livery barn. A photograph of the four bodies became one of the most famous images of frontier vigilante justice.

jim-younger.bio: James Hardin Younger rode with Quantrill's guerrillas as a teenager and joined his brothers in the James-Younger Gang. In March 1874 he was with his brother John in the Roscoe gunfight with Pinkerton agents, where John was killed. At Northfield in 1876 part of his jaw was shot away, and he was captured with Cole and Bob near Madelia. He spent 25 years in Stillwater prison. Paroled in 1901 with Cole, he fell in love with a writer named Alix Muller, but his parole terms did not allow him to marry. Depressed and in pain from his old wounds, he shot himself in a St. Paul hotel room in October 1902.

joaquin-murrieta.bio: Joaquin Murrieta was a Mexican miner from Sonora who came to California during the Gold Rush. Stories say Anglo miners drove him off his claim, beat him and assaulted his wife, and that he turned to banditry for revenge, though much of his story comes from later legend. In 1853 California hired Captain Harry Love and the California State Rangers to hunt down 'the five Joaquins.' In July they killed a man they said was Murrieta, along with Three-Fingered Jack, and cut off his head, which they preserved in a jar and exhibited for years. Whether the head was really his was doubted even then. A popular 1854 novel turned him into a romantic hero, and he is often named as an inspiration for Zorro.

john-chisum.bio:
John Simpson Chisum was born in Tennessee and moved with his family to Paris, Texas, as a boy. He worked as a building contractor and county clerk before going into cattle in the 1850s. After the Civil War he drove herds west to New Mexico, sometimes in partnership with Charles Goodnight, and by the 1870s ran one of the largest cattle operations in the country from his South Spring Ranch near Roswell. His Jinglebob earmark was known across the Southwest, and his herds were said to number more than 100,000 head.

Rustlers and the Murphy–Dolan House were his enemies, and he backed Tunstall and McSween in the Lincoln County War, though he stayed out of the shooting. Billy the Kid later claimed Chisum owed him wages and stole Chisum cattle to collect. Chisum then helped get Pat Garrett elected sheriff. He never married. He died in 1884 after surgery for a growth on his jaw, and was buried in the family plot in Paris, Texas. He is not to be confused with Jesse Chisholm of the Chisholm Trail.

john-heath.bio:
John Heath was a Texas saloon owner with a shady past who came to Bisbee, Arizona, in 1883 and opened a dance hall. He is believed to have planned the robbery of the Goldwater & Castañeda store on December 8, 1883, expecting the Copper Queen mine payroll to be there. When the robbery turned into the Bisbee Massacre, Heath stayed in town and joined the posse, then tried to steer it in the wrong direction, which made Deputy Billy Daniels suspicious.

He was tried separately from the five gunmen and convicted of second-degree murder, which outraged the town. On February 22, 1884, a mob from Bisbee took him from the Tombstone jail and hanged him from a telegraph pole. The coroner famously ruled that he died of 'emphysema of the lungs, which might have been caused by strangulation, self-inflicted or otherwise.'

john-henry-holliday.bio:
John Henry Holliday was born into a well-off family in Griffin, Georgia. His mother died of tuberculosis when he was 15. He earned a degree from the Pennsylvania College of Dental Surgery in 1872 and practiced briefly in Atlanta, but within a year he was diagnosed with the same disease that had killed his mother. Told a dry climate might extend his life, he moved to Dallas in 1873 and opened a dental practice that slowly gave way to gambling, the trade that would carry him across the West.

He drifted through Texas, Colorado and Wyoming, picking up a reputation for a hot temper. At Fort Griffin in 1877 he met Big Nose Kate, his companion on and off for years, and Wyatt Earp. In Dodge City in 1878 Wyatt credited Doc with saving his life when a group of cowboys got the drop on him. Doc followed the Earps to Tombstone in 1880 and stood with them at the O.K. Corral, where he is believed to have killed Tom McLaury with a shotgun. He rode on the Vendetta Ride in 1882. Arrested in Denver that May, he was kept from extradition to Arizona partly through Bat Masterson's efforts.

His last years were spent in Colorado gambling halls in Denver and Leadville, where in 1884 he shot bartender Billy Allen over a small debt and was acquitted. As his health failed he went to Glenwood Springs, hoping the sulfur springs would help, and died at the Hotel Glenwood on November 8, 1887, at age 36. His exact grave in Linwood Cemetery is unknown.

He went on to an unusually varied life: he served briefly as Amarillo's sheriff, went to the Klondike in 1897, served with the Oregon Volunteers in the Philippines, sat in the Oregon legislature and became mayor of Haines, Oregon. He died in 1942 as the last living participant in the fight.

john-selman.bio: John Henry Selman was born in Arkansas and grew up in Texas. He deserted from the Confederate Army and became a lawman and vigilante around Fort Griffin, then led a band of rustlers and killers known as 'Selman's Scouts' in New Mexico during the Lincoln County troubles. He later settled in El Paso, where he became a constable. On August 19, 1895, he shot John Wesley Hardin in the back of the head in the Acme Saloon and was tried and released after a hung jury. Less than a year later, on April 5, 1896, Deputy U.S. Marshal George Scarborough shot him in an alley after an argument, and he died the next day.

john-slaughter.bio: John Horton Slaughter was born in Louisiana and raised in Texas, where he served in the Confederate Army and the Texas Rangers. He became a cattleman and drove herds to New Mexico and Arizona. In 1884 he bought the San Bernardino Ranch on the Mexican border. In 1886 he was elected Cochise County sheriff to clean up the rustling and outlaws left after the Earp era, and he was quietly effective, more than once returning from manhunts without his prisoner. He escorted Buckskin Frank Leslie to the Yuma prison. He later served in the territorial legislature and ranched until his death in Douglas in 1922. His ranch is now a museum.

john-tunstall.bio:
John Henry Tunstall was born in London to a well-off merchant family. After working in his father's business in Canada, he set out in 1876, at 23, to make his fortune in the American West and settled in Lincoln County, New Mexico. With lawyer Alexander McSween, and with backing from cattleman John Chisum, he opened a store and bank in Lincoln that directly challenged the monopoly of Lawrence Murphy and James Dolan's 'House.'

He hired tough young cowboys, including Billy the Kid, to work his ranch on the Rio Feliz. On February 18, 1878, a sheriff's posse sent to seize his horses over a debt claim against McSween caught up with him on the trail and shot him dead. Members of the Jesse Evans Gang were among the killers. His murder started the Lincoln County War. He was 24 and is buried behind his store in Lincoln, now a state historic site.

He is buried next to McSween behind the old Tunstall Store, which is now part of Lincoln Historic Site. A monument and marker stand at the site of his murder southeast of Lincoln.

john-wesley-hardin.bio:
John Wesley Hardin was born in Bonham, Texas, the son of a Methodist preacher who named him after the founder of Methodism. At 15 he shot and killed a freed slave named Mage in an argument, and he spent the Reconstruction years on the run, killing soldiers and state police officers who came after him. He went up the trail to Abilene in 1871, where Marshal Wild Bill Hickok tolerated him. That is where the story arose that he shot a man for snoring through a hotel wall.

He fought on the Taylor side of the Sutton–Taylor feud in South Texas. On his 21st birthday, May 26, 1874, he killed Deputy Sheriff Charles Webb in Comanche, Texas, and fled to Florida under a false name. Texas Ranger John B. Armstrong captured him on a train in Pensacola in 1877. Sentenced to 25 years, he studied law in Huntsville prison and was pardoned in 1894.

He moved to El Paso to practice law, but went back to drinking and gambling. On August 19, 1895, Constable John Selman walked into the Acme Saloon and shot him in the back of the head as he played dice. He claimed to have killed more than 40 men; historians count about 27. His autobiography came out the year after his death.

john-younger.bio: John Harrison Younger was the youngest of the Younger brothers in the gang and had a reputation as the fastest and most reckless. As a teenager he reportedly killed a man in Missouri, and in Dallas in 1873 he shot a sheriff's deputy. On March 17, 1874, near Roscoe, Missouri, he and Jim were confronted by two Pinkerton agents and a local deputy. John killed Deputy Edwin Daniels and mortally wounded agent Louis Lull, but Lull shot him in the neck and he died in the road. He was 23.

johnny-behan.bio:
John Harris Behan was born in Westport, Missouri, and came to Arizona as a young man, serving as sheriff of Yavapai County and in the territorial legislature. When Cochise County was created in 1881 he was appointed its first sheriff, beating Wyatt Earp for the job. He sympathized with the Cowboy faction, was Josephine Marcus's partner before she left him for Wyatt, and was an Earp rival in nearly every way.

Minutes before the O.K. Corral gunfight he tried to stop the Earps on Fremont Street, telling them he had disarmed the Cowboys, which he had not. He then testified against the Earps at the Spicer hearing and later led a posse, which included several Cowboys, in pursuit of Wyatt during the Vendetta Ride. He was not re-elected. He later held government jobs, including at the Yuma Territorial Prison, and served in the Spanish-American War. He died in Tucson in 1912.

johnny-ringo.bio:
John Peters Ringo was born in Greens Fork, Indiana, and was 14 when his family set out for California by wagon in 1864. On the way his father accidentally shot himself to death in front of the family. In the 1870s Ringo turned up in Texas as a gunman in the Mason County 'Hoo Doo' War, a bloody feud between German settlers and Anglo cattlemen, and spent time in jail.

By 1879 he was in Arizona, where he shot a man in a saloon for refusing a drink and became one of the leading figures of the Cowboy faction. Educated, moody and a heavy drinker, he grew into a legend as the 'Cowboy King' after his death. In January 1882 he stood in the street in Tombstone and challenged Doc Holliday to a duel, which police broke up before shots were fired.

In July 1882 he was found dead in West Turkey Creek Canyon, sitting in the fork of a tree, with a bullet hole in his head and his revolver in his hand. The coroner ruled it suicide. Wyatt Earp, Doc Holliday, Buckskin Frank Leslie and gambler Johnny O'Rourke have all been suggested as the killer. He is buried near where he was found.

josephine-marcus.bio:
Josephine Sarah Marcus was born in Brooklyn to German Jewish immigrants and grew up in San Francisco. As a teenager she ran off with a traveling theater troupe and ended up in Arizona, where she became the companion of Johnny Behan, the future Cochise County sheriff, and moved to Tombstone as his common-law wife.

She left Behan in 1881 and became involved with Wyatt Earp, a rivalry that may have added fuel to the feud between the Earps and Behan. She joined Wyatt in California after he left Arizona, and they stayed together for the rest of his life, nearly 47 years, following gold and silver booms to Idaho, Alaska and Nevada. Whether they were ever legally married is uncertain.

After Wyatt died she fought to protect his reputation and tried to control how writers told his story. A memoir published in 1976 as 'I Married Wyatt Earp' has largely been discredited. She died in Los Angeles in 1944 and is buried beside Wyatt in a Jewish cemetery in Colma, California.

josiah-scurlock.bio: Josiah Gordon 'Doc' Scurlock was born in Alabama and reportedly studied medicine, which is where his nickname came from. He came to New Mexico in the early 1870s and ranched with Charlie Bowdre. He was a leader of the Regulators after Dick Brewer's death and fought at the Battle of Lincoln. He left New Mexico in 1879, settled in Texas, raised a large family and worked as a teacher and postmaster, living quietly until his death in Eastland in 1929. He was one of the longest-lived Regulators.

king-fisher.bio: John King Fisher was born in Collin County, Texas, and was a rustler and gunman in his teens. He set up a ranch near Eagle Pass in South Texas, where he led a band of rustlers and supposedly posted a sign at a fork in the road: 'This is King Fisher's road. Take the other one.' He was known for his flashy clothes, including a tiger-skin pair of chaps. He was arrested many times but never convicted. Later he settled down and served as acting sheriff of Uvalde County. On March 11, 1884, he was with Ben Thompson at the Vaudeville Theater in San Antonio when both were killed in an ambush. He is buried in Uvalde.

lawrence-murphy.bio:
Lawrence Gustave Murphy was born in County Wexford, Ireland, and served in the U.S. Army for years before the Civil War and in a New Mexico volunteer regiment during it, earning the title 'Major.' After the war he went into business supplying Fort Stanton and the Mescalero Apache reservation. When the Army threw him off the post for his dealings, he moved to Lincoln and built the two-story store known as the House.

With help from the Santa Fe Ring, Murphy controlled credit, contracts and much of the local government in Lincoln County. By the time the Lincoln County War broke out he was sick with cancer and had turned the business over to James Dolan and John Riley. He spent his final months in Santa Fe and died there in October 1878. His store later became the Lincoln County Courthouse, the building Billy the Kid escaped from.

luke-short.bio:
Luke Lee Short was born in Mississippi and raised on the Texas frontier, where he worked as a cowboy. He sold whiskey to the Sioux, worked as an Army courier and scout and then turned to gambling, which became his trade for life. A small, sharply dressed man, he dealt cards at the Oriental Saloon in Tombstone, where in February 1881 he killed gambler Charlie Storms in a street fight.

In 1883 he bought into the Long Branch Saloon in Dodge City, and when the town's political faction tried to run him out, his friends Wyatt Earp and Bat Masterson came to back him up. The standoff, known as the Dodge City War, ended without bloodshed. He moved to Fort Worth and bought into the White Elephant Saloon. On February 8, 1887, he faced former marshal Jim Courtright, who ran a protection racket, outside the White Elephant and shot him dead. He died of dropsy in Geuda Springs, Kansas, in 1893, at 39, and is buried in Fort Worth's Oakwood Cemetery.

martha-jane-canary.bio:
Martha Jane Canary was born in Missouri; she later gave her birth year as 1852, though it may have been a few years later. Her family went west to the Montana gold fields in the 1860s, and both parents were dead by 1867, leaving her to care for her younger siblings. She took whatever work she could find, as a cook, laundress, dance hall girl, ox team driver and sometimes prostitute. She also dressed as a man and attached herself to Army expeditions, which she would later tell as stories of scouting with Custer.

She arrived in Deadwood in the summer of 1876 with Wild Bill Hickok's party, weeks before his murder. She later claimed they had been married and had a daughter, which historians reject. In Deadwood she earned real affection by nursing smallpox victims during an epidemic. She spent her later years drinking heavily and touring in dime museums and at the 1901 Pan-American Exposition. She died in Terry, South Dakota, in 1903 and, at her request, was buried next to Hickok in Mount Moriah Cemetery.

morgan-earp.bio:
Morgan Seth Earp was born in Pella, Iowa, the youngest of the brothers who went to Tombstone, and by most accounts the most easygoing. He worked as a lawman in Dodge City and Butte, Montana, before joining Wyatt and Virgil in Arizona in 1880, where he rode shotgun for Wells Fargo and served as a special deputy under Virgil. At the O.K. Corral he was shot through both shoulders.

On the night of March 18, 1882, Morgan was playing billiards at Campbell & Hatch's saloon in Tombstone when shots fired through a back door window struck him in the spine. He died within the hour, at age 30, with Wyatt and his brothers at his side. Frank Stilwell, Pete Spence and others were named as suspects. His murder set off Wyatt's Vendetta Ride. His body was sent to his parents in Colton, California, where he is buried.

ned-christie.bio:
Ned Christie was a Cherokee gunsmith, blacksmith and member of the Cherokee National Council. In 1887 Deputy U.S. Marshal Dan Maples was shot and killed near Tahlequah, and Christie was accused. He refused to surrender to a white court, saying he would not get a fair trial, and built a fortified log house near Wauhillau where he held off marshals for nearly five years.

On November 3, 1892, a large posse used a small cannon and finally dynamite to blow up his fort. Christie was shot as he ran from it. In 1918 an eyewitness came forward to say another man had killed Maples, and Christie is widely regarded today as a Cherokee patriot who was wrongly accused.

oliver-loving.bio:
Oliver Loving was born in Hopkins County, Kentucky, and moved his family to Texas in the 1840s, settling in what became Palo Pinto County. He farmed, freighted and raised cattle, and he was one of the first Texans to drive herds to distant markets: to Louisiana, to Chicago in 1858 and to the Colorado gold fields at Denver in 1860, where the Civil War stranded him for a time. During the war he supplied beef to the Confederacy.

In 1866 he joined forces with the younger Charles Goodnight, and they drove their combined herd across the dry country to Fort Sumner, New Mexico, where the Army bought the steers for $12,000 in gold. Loving drove the rest north to Colorado.

On the second drive in 1867, Loving rode ahead with 'One-Armed' Bill Wilson to arrange the sale and was trapped by a Comanche war party along the Pecos River. Wounded in the arm and side, he held them off while Wilson slipped away to get help, then hid and crawled to safety until Mexican traders carried him to Fort Sumner. He put off amputating the arm until too late and died of gangrene on September 25, 1867. Goodnight brought his body home to Weatherford for burial.

patrick-garrett.bio:
Patrick Floyd Jarvis Garrett was born in Alabama and raised on a Louisiana plantation that the Civil War ruined. He went to Texas as a cowboy and buffalo hunter, where he killed a fellow hunter, Joe Briscoe, in a dispute, and drifted to Fort Sumner, New Mexico, around 1878. At six foot four he stood out, and he knew Billy the Kid there socially.

With the backing of cattlemen like John Chisum, he was elected Lincoln County sheriff in 1880 to clean up rustling. He captured the Kid at Stinking Springs that December, and after the Kid's escape from Lincoln he killed him at Pete Maxwell's house on July 14, 1881. The next year he published 'The Authentic Life of Billy the Kid,' largely ghostwritten by Ash Upson, which created much of the Kid's legend. It did little for Garrett's own popularity, as many locals felt he had shot the Kid without warning.

His later career was uneven. He led a ranger company in the Texas Panhandle, failed at irrigation schemes, and as Doña Ana County sheriff investigated the 1896 disappearance of Albert Fountain and his son. Theodore Roosevelt appointed him customs collector at El Paso in 1901. Deep in debt, he was shot and killed on a road outside Las Cruces on February 29, 1908, during a quarrel over a land lease. Wayne Brazel confessed and was acquitted on self-defense. Many suspect the hired killer Jim Miller.

pearl-hart.bio: Pearl Hart was born Pearl Taylor in Lindsay, Ontario, and eloped as a teenager with a gambler named Hart, who abused her. She drifted to Arizona, working at odd jobs, and in May 1899 she and a miner named Joe Boot robbed the Globe-to-Florence stagecoach, one of the last stage robberies in the West. They were caught within days. Her story made her a newspaper sensation, and she served time in the Yuma Territorial Prison until 1902. Afterward she briefly performed on stage as 'The Arizona Bandit' and then disappeared from view. Where she died is uncertain.

pete-spence.bio:
Pete Spence was the alias of Elliot Larkin Ferguson, a former Texas Ranger who fled Texas under suspicion and settled in Tombstone, where he lived across the street from the Earps. He was arrested with Frank Stilwell for the Bisbee stage robbery in 1881. His wife told the coroner's inquest that Spence and others had planned Morgan Earp's murder, but her testimony was not admissible against her husband and he was never tried.

Wyatt's posse killed Spence's woodcutter friend Florentino Cruz during the Vendetta Ride while Spence himself was in jail for his own protection. Spence later served time in the Yuma prison for killing a man, then settled near Globe. He married the widow of Fin Clanton, died in 1914 and is buried beside Fin in Globe Cemetery.

phineas-clanton.bio: Phineas 'Fin' Clanton was the eldest son of Newman 'Old Man' Clanton and the quietest of the Clanton brothers. He was not in Tombstone for the O.K. Corral gunfight but rode with Sheriff Behan's posse against the Earps during the Vendetta Ride. In 1887 he was convicted of cattle rustling and served time in the Yuma Territorial Prison. After his release he settled near Globe, Arizona, and lived as a rancher and goat herder until he died of pneumonia in 1906.
