red-sample.bio: Omer W. 'Red' Sample was one of the five Bisbee raiders and, like Dan Dowd, stood guard outside the store shooting at anyone on the street. He was caught at Clifton, Arizona, along with Tex Howard. A gold watch taken in the robbery was found on him, which helped convict him. He was hanged in Tombstone on March 28, 1884.

richard-m-brewer.bio: Richard 'Dick' Brewer was born in Vermont and grew up in Wisconsin before coming to New Mexico, where he farmed on the Rio Ruidoso and became foreman of John Tunstall's ranch. He was well liked and considered steady and honest. After Tunstall's murder he was made a special constable, which gave the Regulators the color of law, and he led them as their first captain. At Blazer's Mill on April 4, 1878, the badly wounded Buckshot Roberts shot him through the head from inside a building. He was 27.

robert-clay-allison.bio:
Robert Clay Allison was born in Tennessee and served in the Confederate Army, from which he was discharged for what an Army doctor described as emotional or mental instability. After the war he went to Texas and then to Colfax County, New Mexico, where he ranched and became known as a dangerous man when drinking. He led a lynch mob in Elizabethtown in 1870 that hanged a suspected murderer.

In January 1874, at the Clifton House, he shot gunman Chunk Colbert during or after dinner; Colbert had drawn his pistol under the table. He played a violent part in the Colfax County War and killed several more men. Allison later ranched in Texas. He died on July 1, 1887, near Pecos, when he fell off a loaded freight wagon and was run over by its wheel.

robert-ford.bio:
Robert Newton Ford was born in Virginia and grew up in Missouri. He idolized Jesse James as a boy, and in 1882 he and his brother Charley joined Jesse's new gang. Bob secretly made a deal with Governor Thomas Crittenden for a reward. On April 3, 1882, while Jesse was standing on a chair in his own home, Bob shot him in the back of the head.

The brothers were convicted of murder, sentenced to hang and pardoned by Crittenden the same day, but they received only a small part of the reward. Bob reenacted the killing on stage and was widely despised as a coward. He drifted west, ran saloons in Colorado and settled in the boomtown of Creede. On June 8, 1892, Edward O'Kelley walked into his tent saloon and killed him with a shotgun. His grave in Richmond, Missouri, is marked 'The man who shot Jesse James.'

robert-leroy-parker.bio:
Robert LeRoy Parker was born in Beaver, Utah, the oldest of 13 children in a Mormon family, and grew up on a ranch near Circleville. As a teenager he fell under the influence of a cattle rustler named Mike Cassidy, whose name he later borrowed; 'Butch' came from a stint working in a butcher shop. In 1889 he joined Matt Warner and Tom McCarty in robbing a bank in Telluride, Colorado.

He served 18 months in the Wyoming penitentiary for horse theft and was pardoned in 1896, reportedly after promising the governor he would leave Wyoming alone. He then built the Wild Bunch, a loose group of outlaws who hid out at Hole-in-the-Wall, Brown's Park and Robbers Roost. They robbed the Montpelier, Idaho, bank in 1896, the Castle Gate, Utah, mine payroll in 1897, and Union Pacific trains at Wilcox (1899) and Tipton (1900), as well as a bank in Winnemucca, Nevada. Butch was well liked and claimed he never killed anyone during his years in the United States.

With the Pinkertons closing in, he left for New York and then Argentina in 1901 with the Sundance Kid and Etta Place. They ranched in Patagonia for several years before going back to robbery. In November 1908, after a mining payroll was robbed in Bolivia, the two Americans were cornered in the village of San Vicente. Bolivian reports say they died there, apparently Butch killing Sundance and then himself. His sister Lula insisted he came home and lived quietly for decades, but no evidence has confirmed it.

roy-bean.bio:
Phantly Roy Bean Jr. was born in Mason County, Kentucky, around 1825. He left home as a teenager and spent the 1840s and 1850s drifting through Mexico, San Diego and Southern California, where his brother Joshua was the first mayor of San Diego. Roy got into duels, was jailed and escaped, and supposedly survived a botched hanging by a romantic rival's friends. During the Civil War he ran a freight and blockade business in Texas for the Confederacy, and afterward he lived in San Antonio running a string of shady businesses.

In 1882 he followed railroad construction crews to the Pecos River and opened a tent saloon. He was appointed justice of the peace, and he held court in his saloon, the Jersey Lilly at Langtry, calling himself 'The Law West of the Pecos.' He mostly fined people and kept the money, and the stories of his odd rulings made him famous.

He admired British actress Lillie Langtry and wrote to her for years. In 1896 he staged a heavyweight championship fight between Bob Fitzsimmons and Peter Maher on a sandbar in the Rio Grande to get around Texas's ban on prizefighting. He died in March 1903 after a drinking binge in Del Rio. Lillie Langtry visited the town ten months later.

He was first buried in Westlawn Cemetery in Del Rio and is now on the grounds of the Whitehead Memorial Museum (1308 S. Main St., Del Rio), next to his son Sam and a replica of the Jersey Lilly.

sam-bass.bio:
Sam Bass was born in Mitchell, Indiana, and orphaned by 13. He went to Texas in 1870, worked as a cowboy and teamster in Denton, and made money racing a fast horse called the Denton Mare. In 1876 he and Joel Collins drove a herd to Kansas and Nebraska, lost the money gambling in the Black Hills, and turned to robbing stagecoaches.

On September 18, 1877, the gang robbed a Union Pacific train at Big Springs, Nebraska, and took about $60,000 in new $20 gold pieces, the biggest Union Pacific robbery up to that time. Collins and others were killed soon afterward, but Bass made it back to Texas, where he robbed four trains around Dallas in 1878.

Texas Rangers turned gang member Jim Murphy into an informant. When the gang arrived to rob the bank at Round Rock, the Rangers were waiting. Bass was shot on July 19, 1878, and died two days later, on his 27th birthday. He is buried in Round Rock. Folk songs about him circulated for decades, and stories of his buried gold persist.

seth-bullock.bio:
Seth Bullock was born in Amherstburg, Ontario, and went to Montana as a young man, where he served in the territorial senate and as sheriff of Lewis and Clark County. In August 1876, the day after Wild Bill Hickok was killed, he and his partner Sol Star arrived in Deadwood to open a hardware store. Deadwood had no law, and Bullock became its first sheriff when Lawrence County was organized in 1877.

He went into ranching, mining and business, and in 1884, while working as a deputy U.S. marshal, he met another deputy, Theodore Roosevelt, beginning a lifelong friendship. He served as a captain in a volunteer cavalry regiment during the Spanish-American War, rode in Roosevelt's inaugural parade and was appointed U.S. Marshal for South Dakota. He built the Bullock Hotel in Deadwood, which still stands. When Roosevelt died in 1919, Bullock built a memorial tower on Mount Roosevelt above Deadwood. He died eight months later and is buried at Mount Moriah facing the tower.

sherman-mcmaster.bio: Sherman McMaster was born in Illinois and served briefly with the Texas Rangers before coming to Arizona, where his loyalties were unusually mixed. He knew Curly Bill and the Cowboys and was suspected in a stagecoach robbery, yet he worked as an informant for the Earps and rode with Wyatt on the Vendetta Ride. He left Arizona with the posse. Wyatt later claimed McMaster died in the Philippines during the Spanish-American War, but a family probate record indicates he died in Colorado in 1892.

tex-howard.bio: James 'Tex' Howard came to Bisbee with John Heath and was one of the men who went inside the Goldwater & Castañeda store during the robbery of December 8, 1883. He did not wear a mask, so witnesses could identify him quickly. He was arrested at Clifton, Arizona, with Red Sample, convicted of murder in Tombstone and hanged on March 28, 1884.

texas-jack-omohundro.bio:
John Baker Omohundro was born on a farm in Fluvanna County, Virginia. At 17 he joined the Confederate cavalry under J.E.B. Stuart, serving as a courier and scout. After the war he went to Texas as a cowboy, which earned him his nickname, and helped drive cattle north. In Nebraska he became an Army scout alongside Buffalo Bill Cody, and the two became close friends.

In December 1872 dime novelist Ned Buntline put both scouts on stage in Chicago in 'The Scouts of the Prairie,' with Italian ballerina Giuseppina Morlacchi. Critics mocked it, but audiences loved it, and Texas Jack married Morlacchi in 1873. He went on to lead his own touring company and wrote about hunting and the frontier.

In 1880 the couple went to the Leadville silver boom, where he caught pneumonia and died on June 28 at age 33. Buffalo Bill later paid for a granite marker for his grave in Evergreen Cemetery.

thomas-ketchem.bio:
Thomas Edward Ketchum was born in San Saba County, Texas, and worked as a cowboy before turning to crime with his brother Sam in the 1890s. The Black Jack gang robbed trains, stores and post offices across New Mexico, Arizona and Texas, and Tom was suspected of several murders. In 1899 Sam was mortally wounded after a train robbery near Folsom, New Mexico, and later died in the territorial prison.

A month later Tom tried to rob the same train near Folsom by himself. The conductor, Frank Harrington, shot him in the arm with a shotgun, and the arm had to be amputated. New Mexico had made attempted train robbery a hanging offense, and he was hanged in Clayton on April 26, 1901. The rope was too long and the drop pulled his head off. He reportedly told the crowd before the drop, 'I'll be in hell before you start breakfast, boys.'

tiburcio-vasquez.bio: Tiburcio Vásquez was born in Monterey, California, to a respected Californio family. He turned to crime as a young man and spent years in and out of San Quentin, robbing stagecoaches, stores and travelers across central California. He presented himself as a defender of Mexican Californians against Anglo injustice, and many Hispanic Californians protected him. In 1873 his gang's robbery at Tres Pinos left three men dead. He was captured in 1874 at a hideout in what is now West Hollywood, convicted of murder and hanged in San Jose on March 19, 1875.

tom-bear-river-smith.bio:
Thomas James Smith was born in New York City and worked as a prizefighter and a New York police officer before going west with the Union Pacific railroad crews. In 1868 he helped calm the Bear River Riot in Wyoming, which gave him his nickname. He served as marshal in railroad towns including Kit Carson, Colorado.

In 1870 Abilene, Kansas, hired him as its first marshal. He enforced a ban on carrying guns in town, and he usually disarmed troublemakers with his fists instead of his revolvers. He was respected even by the Texas cowboys. On November 2, 1870, while serving a murder warrant on a homesteader near Abilene, he was shot and then nearly beheaded with an axe. Wild Bill Hickok took over the job the next year. President Dwight Eisenhower, who grew up in Abilene, admired Smith and visited his grave.

tom-horn.bio:
Thomas Horn Jr. was born in Memphis, Missouri, and ran away at 16 after a beating from his father. He went to the Southwest and worked for the Army as a scout, packer and interpreter during the Apache Wars, and was involved in the negotiations around Geronimo's surrender in 1886. He then worked as a cowboy, rodeo roper, deputy and Pinkerton detective in Colorado.

In the 1890s Wyoming cattlemen hired him as a 'range detective,' killing suspected rustlers for pay. In July 1901, 14-year-old Willie Nickell was shot near his family's ranch, possibly mistaken for his father. Deputy U.S. Marshal Joe LeFors got Horn to talk about it while drinking, with a stenographer listening behind a door. Horn was convicted on that confession and hanged in Cheyenne on November 20, 1903, the day before his 43rd birthday. He wrote his autobiography in jail. Whether he really killed the boy is still debated, and a mock retrial in 1993 acquitted him.

tom-mclaury.bio:
Thomas Clark McLaury was born in Kortright, New York, the younger brother of Frank and partner in the family's Arizona cattle business. The day of the O.K. Corral gunfight, Wyatt Earp pistol-whipped him on the street after a confrontation. Whether Tom was armed when the fight began that afternoon is still one of the most disputed points of the whole affair. Witnesses friendly to the Cowboys swore he threw open his coat to show he had no gun.

He was killed by a shotgun blast, almost certainly fired by Doc Holliday, as he stood near his brother's horse. He was 28. He is buried in Tombstone's Boothill beside his brother and Billy Clanton.

tom-o-folliard.bio: Tom O'Folliard was born in Uvalde, Texas, and lost both parents to smallpox in Mexico as a child. He came to Lincoln County in 1878, where he became Billy the Kid's closest friend and constant companion. He fought in the Battle of Lincoln and rode with the Kid as a rustler afterward. On December 19, 1880, Pat Garrett's posse ambushed the gang as they rode into Fort Sumner, and O'Folliard was shot through the chest. He died about 45 minutes later. He was 22 and is buried with the Kid and Charlie Bowdre at Fort Sumner.

virgil-earp.bio:
Virgil Walter Earp was born in Hartford, Kentucky, the older brother who often led where Wyatt followed. As a teenager he eloped with a Dutch girl, Ellen Rysdam; her family broke up the marriage while he was away in the Union Army, and he did not learn until decades later that he had a daughter from it. After the war he drove freight and stagecoaches across the West and served as a night watchman and constable in Prescott, Arizona.

In 1879 he was appointed a deputy U.S. marshal for southern Arizona and moved to Tombstone, bringing his brothers along. He became Tombstone's town marshal in 1881, and it was Virgil, not Wyatt, who was the lawman in charge when he walked down Fremont Street on October 26 to disarm the Cowboys. He was shot through the calf at the O.K. Corral. Two months later, on December 28, 1881, he was ambushed with shotguns on Allen Street, which left his left arm permanently crippled.

He recovered in California, later serving as the first city marshal of Colton. He spent his last years in the Nevada mining camps and died of pneumonia in Goldfield in 1905. His daughter from his first marriage had him buried in Portland, Oregon.

warren-earp.bio:
Warren Baxter Earp was the youngest of the Earp brothers, born in Pella, Iowa, in 1855. He came to Tombstone in 1881, too late for the O.K. Corral, and rode with Wyatt on the Vendetta Ride in 1882 after Morgan's murder. He was known as a hothead without his older brothers' judgment.

He later drifted back to Arizona and worked as a stage driver and range rider around Willcox. On July 6, 1900, he quarreled with cowboy Johnny Boyett in a Willcox saloon and was shot dead; he was unarmed, and Boyett was never convicted. He is the only Earp brother buried in Arizona.

william-brady.bio:
William J. Brady was born in County Cavan, Ireland, and came to America in 1851, enlisting in the U.S. Army right away. He served through the Civil War with New Mexico volunteer units, rising to captain, and stayed in New Mexico afterward, farming near Lincoln and serving in the territorial legislature. He became Lincoln County's sheriff and was closely tied to his fellow Irishmen Lawrence Murphy and James Dolan.

In February 1878 he sent the posse that killed John Tunstall. On April 1, 1878, as he walked down Lincoln's main street with his deputies, Regulators hiding behind the wall of Tunstall's corral opened fire and killed him and Deputy George Hindman. Billy the Kid was later convicted of his murder. Brady left a widow and nine children. He is buried on what was once his ranch east of Lincoln.
william-brady.dateNote: Some sources give his birth year as 1825.
incidents: Sent the posse that killed Tunstall

legends.text: Killed by Billy the Kid personally

william-brady.name: William J. Brady
william-brady.notes: Irish immigrant and Army veteran who served in the territorial legislature before becoming sheriff. He sided with the Murphy–Dolan faction. About seven Regulators fired on him, and no one knows whose shots killed him; Billy the Kid was later convicted of his murder. He is buried with Deputy George Hindman on private land east of Lincoln.
william-brady.resting: Brady–Hindman burial site, on Brady's old ranch east of Lincoln, NM (private property)

william-brocius.bio:
Nobody knows for certain where Curly Bill Brocius came from or what his real name was; one theory is that he was a William Graham from Missouri or Texas. He appeared in Arizona around 1878 and became the most notorious of the Cochise County Cowboys, a hard-drinking, practical-joking rustler who was both feared and, by some, liked.

In October 1880 Tombstone Marshal Fred White tried to disarm him and was mortally wounded when Curly Bill's pistol went off. Wyatt Earp clubbed him over the head and arrested him. White's deathbed statement that the shooting was an accident got Curly Bill acquitted, but it left bad blood with the Earps.

On March 24, 1882, during the Vendetta Ride, Wyatt said he killed Curly Bill with a shotgun at Iron Springs in the Whetstone Mountains. The Cowboys denied it and the Tombstone Nugget offered money for proof he was dead, but he was never seen again. His grave, if he has one, is unknown.

william-cody.bio:
William Frederick Cody was born in Le Claire, Iowa, and grew up in Kansas. His father, an antislavery settler, died when Bill was 11, and Bill went to work as a boy, possibly including a stint with the Pony Express, though that story is disputed. He served as a Union soldier in the Civil War and then hunted buffalo to feed Kansas Pacific railroad crews, which earned him his nickname. As an Army scout he took part in many fights with Plains tribes and was awarded the Medal of Honor in 1872.

Dime novelist Ned Buntline made him a hero in print and put him on stage in 1872 in 'The Scouts of the Prairie' with Texas Jack Omohundro. In 1876, scouting for the 5th Cavalry after Little Bighorn, he killed the Cheyenne warrior Yellow Hair and later reenacted it on stage.

In 1883 he launched Buffalo Bill's Wild West, which grew into the most famous show of its time, with Annie Oakley, Sitting Bull for one season and hundreds of cowboys and American Indian performers. It toured Europe and performed for Queen Victoria in 1887. He founded the town of Cody, Wyoming, but lost much of his fortune in bad investments. He died in Denver in 1917 and is buried on Lookout Mountain above Golden, Colorado.

william-h-bonney.bio:
Billy the Kid was born Henry McCarty, most likely in New York City, around 1859. His mother, Catherine, took him and his brother west through Indiana and Kansas and married William Antrim in Santa Fe in 1873, settling in the mining town of Silver City, New Mexico. She died of tuberculosis in 1874, leaving Henry, then about 14, mostly on his own. Arrested for stealing clothes in 1875, he escaped the Silver City jail by climbing up the chimney and fled to Arizona. There, in August 1877, he shot blacksmith Windy Cahill, his first known killing.

Back in New Mexico, now calling himself William H. Bonney, he went to work for English rancher John Tunstall. Tunstall's murder in February 1878 made the Kid a Regulator in the Lincoln County War. He took part in the ambush of Sheriff William Brady, the fight at Blazer's Mill and the Battle of Lincoln, escaping from the burning McSween house. In 1879 he met secretly with Governor Lew Wallace and agreed to testify in exchange for a pardon that never came. He went back to rustling around Fort Sumner with Tom O'Folliard, Charlie Bowdre and Dave Rudabaugh.

Sheriff Pat Garrett, once a friendly acquaintance, captured him at Stinking Springs in December 1880. Convicted in April 1881 of Brady's murder, the only conviction to come out of the war, he was sentenced to hang. Instead he escaped from the Lincoln courthouse on April 28, killing deputies James Bell and Bob Olinger. Garrett caught up with him at Pete Maxwell's house in Fort Sumner on the night of July 14, 1881, and shot him in a darkened bedroom. He was about 21. Legend credits him with 21 killings; the real number is closer to eight or nine. His only authenticated photograph, a tintype, sold in 2011 for $2.3 million.

windy-cahill.bio: Francis P. 'Windy' Cahill was an Irish-born civilian blacksmith working near Camp Grant, Arizona. He was a big man who enjoyed bullying the slight teenager then known as Kid Antrim, and he had a record of violence of his own. On August 17, 1877, at George Atkins's cantina, Cahill called the Kid a pimp, threw him to the floor and pinned him. The Kid pulled his pistol and shot him in the stomach. Cahill gave a deathbed statement the next day and died. A coroner's jury called the shooting 'criminal and unjustifiable,' and the Kid fled to New Mexico. It was the first known killing by the future Billy the Kid.
incidents: Shot by Billy the Kid at Atkins' Cantina (Aug 17, 1877)

legends.text: Billy the Kid's first known killing

windy-cahill.name: Francis P. Cahill
windy-cahill.notes: Civilian blacksmith at Camp Grant who regularly bullied the teenage Kid. His deathbed statement ran in the Arizona Weekly Star on Aug 23, 1877. Researcher James Townsend found that Cahill had earlier been arrested in Tucson for knifing an Army officer's servant.
windy-cahill.resting: Fort Grant post cemetery, AZ (buried Aug 19, 1877)

wyatt-earp.bio:
Wyatt Berry Stapp Earp was born in Monmouth, Illinois, and grew up in a restless family that moved to Pella, Iowa, and then by wagon to California in 1864. His early adult years were rough. He served as a constable in Lamar, Missouri, where his first wife, Urilla, died within a year of their marriage. He was then arrested for horse theft in Indian Territory in 1871 and skipped bail, and turned up in court records connected with brothels in Peoria. He found steadier footing as a buffalo hunter and then as a police officer in Wichita and Dodge City, where he worked alongside Bat Masterson. While chasing Dave Rudabaugh through Fort Griffin, Texas, in 1877 he met Doc Holliday, beginning the most famous friendship in Western history.

In 1879 Wyatt followed his brother Virgil to the silver boomtown of Tombstone, Arizona, with his brothers Morgan and James. Tension with the Cochise County Cowboys, the Clantons and McLaurys, and with Sheriff Johnny Behan built up through 1881 and exploded at the O.K. Corral on October 26. Afterward Virgil was ambushed and crippled, and Morgan was murdered in March 1882. Wyatt then led a federal posse on the Vendetta Ride, killing Frank Stilwell in Tucson, Curly Bill Brocius at Iron Springs and at least one more suspect before leaving Arizona for good.

He spent the next 47 years with Josephine Marcus, chasing booms from San Diego to Nome, Alaska (where he ran the Dexter Saloon), to Tonopah and Goldfield, Nevada. He raced horses, refereed the controversial 1896 Fitzsimmons–Sharkey fight and in old age befriended early Hollywood cowboy stars in Los Angeles. He died there in January 1929. Stuart Lake's 1931 book 'Wyatt Earp: Frontier Marshal' turned him into the incorruptible lawman of the movies, an image historians have been arguing with ever since.

york-kelly.bio: Daniel 'York' Kelly was one of the five gunmen in the Bisbee Massacre. After the robbery he fled east and was arrested near Deming, New Mexico, reportedly after a barber recognized him from his description while giving him a shave. He was tried in Tombstone and hanged with the others on March 28, 1884. He is buried in Tombstone's Boothill.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Bisbee massacre

abilene.name: Abilene
abilene.summary: Became the end of the Chisholm Trail in 1867. Wild Bill Hickok was its marshal in 1871.

bisbee.name: Bisbee
bisbee.summary: A copper camp in the Mule Mountains with no bank, so the Goldwater & Castaneda store held the miners' payroll. That made it the target of the 1883 Bisbee Massacre.

cimarron.knownFor: Ranching on the Santa Fe Trail
cimarron.name: Cimarron
cimarron.summary: Center of the Colfax County War. Clay Allison's stomping ground; the Clifton House stood nearby.

coffeyville.name: Coffeyville
coffeyville.summary: Townspeople shot down most of the Dalton Gang when it tried to rob two banks at once in 1892.

creede.name: Creede
creede.summary: A silver camp where Bob Ford was shot dead in his tent saloon in 1892.

deadwood.name: Deadwood
deadwood.summary: A Black Hills gold camp settled illegally on Lakota land. Wild Bill Hickok was killed here and Seth Bullock became its first sheriff.

dodge-city.name: Dodge City
dodge-city.summary: A railroad town that shipped buffalo hides and then Texas cattle. Wyatt Earp and the Masterson brothers wore badges here.

el-paso.name: El Paso
el-paso.summary: A border town nicknamed the 'Six-shooter Capital'. Dallas Stoudenmire, John Wesley Hardin and John Selman all died here.

fort-griffin.knownFor: Army post and buffalo-hide town ('The Flat')
fort-griffin.name: Fort Griffin
fort-griffin.summary: A cavalry fort on the Clear Fork of the Brazos, with a wild civilian town below it called The Flat or Hide Town. Wyatt Earp first met Doc Holliday here, and Doc met Big Nose Kate. Today the Fort Griffin State Historic Site, about 15 miles northeast of Albany, TX, has some fort buildings and ruins and a good visitor center. Nothing remains of The Flat itself; a private landowner has built a replica of the town.
fort-griffin.visitNote: Some buildings and ruins of the fort remain, and there's a nice visitor center. Nothing is left of the town; the landowner put up a replica of it.

fort-smith.name: Fort Smith
fort-smith.summary: Seat of Judge Isaac Parker's federal court and its gallows. Deputy marshals rode out from here into Indian Territory.

fort-sumner.knownFor: Army post, later a ranch town
fort-sumner.name: Fort Sumner
fort-sumner.summary: Built as an army post on the Pecos. Pat Garrett killed Billy the Kid here in 1881.

fort-worth.name: Fort Worth
fort-worth.summary: 'Where the West begins.' Its Hell's Half Acre district saw Luke Short kill Jim Courtright in 1887.

glenwood-springs.name: Glenwood Springs
glenwood-springs.summary: Mountain resort town where Doc Holliday died of tuberculosis in 1887.

guthrie.knownFor: Land Run town and territorial capital
guthrie.name: Guthrie
guthrie.summary: Sprang up in a day during the 1889 Land Run. Base of the Three Guardsmen.

holbrook.name: Holbrook
holbrook.summary: Railroad town where Sheriff Commodore Perry Owens fought the Blevins family in 1887.

las-vegas-nm.name: Las Vegas
las-vegas-nm.summary: Railroad boomtown controlled for a time by the 'Dodge City Gang' of Hoodoo Brown, Dave Mather and Dave Rudabaugh.

lincoln.name: Lincoln
lincoln.summary: County seat at the center of the Lincoln County War between the Murphy–Dolan faction and the Regulators.

northfield.name: Northfield
northfield.summary: The James–Younger Gang's 1876 raid here ended with the gang shot to pieces and the Youngers captured.

round-rock.name: Round Rock
round-rock.summary: Sam Bass was shot here in 1878 while scouting the town's bank.

san-antonio.name: San Antonio
san-antonio.summary: Ben Thompson and King Fisher were killed together in its Vaudeville Theater in 1884.

skagway.name: Skagway
skagway.summary: Gateway to the Klondike, run for a time by Soapy Smith's con men until the Juneau Wharf shootout.

st-joseph.knownFor: River trade and the Pony Express
st-joseph.name: St. Joseph
st-joseph.summary: Eastern end of the Pony Express. Bob Ford shot Jesse James in a house here in 1882.

tascosa.name: Tascosa
tascosa.summary: A Panhandle cowtown and hangout for rustlers and cowboys. Its Boot Hill holds the dead of the 1886 Big Fight. The town faded after the railroad passed it by.

tombstone.name: Tombstone
tombstone.summary: A silver boomtown that grew to thousands within a few years. Home of the Earps, the Cochise County Cowboys and the O.K. Corral.

ada-lynching.name: Lynching at Ada
ada-lynching.summary: A mob took Jim Miller and three others from jail and hanged them in a livery barn.

adair-train-robbery.name: Adair Train Robbery
adair-train-robbery.summary: The James-Younger Gang's first train robbery. Wearing Ku Klux Klan masks, they pulled a rail on a blind curve west of Adair and derailed the eastbound Chicago, Rock Island & Pacific. Engineer John Rafferty was killed and fireman Dennis Foley later died of his injuries. They expected a gold shipment but got only about $3,000. A Rock Island locomotive wheel placed in 1954 marks it as the 'first train robbery in the West'; the Reno Gang had already robbed a train in Indiana in 1866. Clell Miller rode along; John and Bob Younger may also have been there.

adobe-walls.name: Second Battle of Adobe Walls
adobe-walls.summary: Buffalo hunters, including a young Bat Masterson, held off a large Comanche and Cheyenne war party.

battle-of-lincoln.name: Battle of Lincoln
battle-of-lincoln.summary: Five-day siege that ended the Lincoln County War with the burning of the McSween house.

bear-river-riot.name: Bear River Riot
bear-river-riot.summary: Union Pacific graders rioted in the hell-on-wheels town of Bear River City, about ten miles southeast of present-day Evanston. Tom Smith's part in it earned him the nickname 'Bear River.' Some sources date it to 1867.

bear-river-smith-killed.name: Killing of Marshal Tom Smith
bear-river-smith-killed.place: Dugout on Chapman Creek, about 10 miles from Abilene, KS
bear-river-smith-killed.summary: Serving a murder warrant on homesteaders Andrew McConnell and Moses Miles, Abilene's first marshal was shot; his deputy fled, and Miles finished him with an axe. Both killers were later convicted. Wild Bill Hickok replaced Smith as marshal.

big-springs.name: Big Springs Robbery
big-springs.summary: Bass and Joel Collins' gang took about $60,000 in new gold coins from a Union Pacific train.

bisbee-five-hanged.name: Hanging of the Bisbee Five
bisbee-five-hanged.summary: The five robbers were hanged together, the largest mass hanging in Arizona history. Nellie Cashman hired miners to guard their Boothill graves from body snatchers for ten days.

bisbee-massacre.name: Bisbee Massacre
bisbee-massacre.summary: Five outlaws came for the Copper Queen Mine payroll, which hadn't arrived yet, and got away with somewhere between $800 and $3,000. The two men posted outside shot down townspeople, killing four people and Annie Roberts' unborn child. The building is now the Letson Loft Hotel.

blazers-mill.name: Gunfight at Blazer's Mill
blazers-mill.summary: Buckshot Roberts held off the Regulators alone, killing Dick Brewer before dying of his wounds.

bob-ford-killed.name: Killing of Bob Ford
bob-ford-killed.summary: Edward O'Kelley killed Ford with a shotgun in his tent saloon.

brady-ambush.name: Ambush of Sheriff William Brady
brady-ambush.summary: April Fool's Day. Regulators hiding in the corral behind Tunstall's store opened fire on Sheriff Brady and his deputies on Lincoln's main street, killing Brady and Deputy George Hindman. The shooters included Billy the Kid, Jim French, Frank McNab, John Middleton, Fred Waite and Henry Brown; no one knows whose shots killed Brady. The Kid ran out to Brady's body, possibly for his confiscated Winchester or the warrants, and was wounded by Deputy Billy Mathews. The ambush cost the Regulators public sympathy. The Kid was later convicted of Brady's murder, the only conviction from the war.

castle-gate.name: Castle Gate Payroll Robbery
castle-gate.summary: Butch Cassidy and Elzy Lay took the coal company's payroll, about $7,000–8,000.

cherokee-bill-hanged.name: Execution of Cherokee Bill
cherokee-bill-hanged.summary: Hanged at Fort Smith on Judge Parker's sentence before hundreds of spectators.

christie-siege.name: Siege of Ned's Fort
christie-siege.summary: A posse used a cannon and dynamite on Ned Christie's fortified cabin and killed him as he ran out.

clifton-house.name: Dinner at the Clifton House
clifton-house.summary: Colbert drew on Allison at dinner, snagged his gun on the table and was shot dead.

coffeyville-raid.name: Coffeyville Raid
coffeyville-raid.summary: The Daltons tried to rob two banks at once. Four gang members died; Emmett survived with many wounds.

doolin-killed.name: Killing of Bill Doolin
doolin-killed.summary: Heck Thomas' posse killed Doolin with a shotgun blast after his jail escape.

earp-meets-holliday.name: Wyatt Earp Meets Doc Holliday
earp-meets-holliday.place: John Shanssey's saloon, Fort Griffin (The Flat), TX
earp-meets-holliday.summary: Hunting Dave Rudabaugh, Wyatt Earp asked his old friend, saloon owner John Shanssey, for help. Shanssey pointed him to a gambler who had played cards with Rudabaugh: Doc Holliday. It began their lifelong friendship. Doc had met Big Nose Kate in the same town shortly before.

fitzsimmons-maher-fight.name: Fitzsimmons–Maher Prizefight
fitzsimmons-maher-fight.place: Rio Grande sandbar near Langtry, TX
fitzsimmons-maher-fight.summary: Prizefighting was banned in Texas and nearby states, so Roy Bean staged the heavyweight bout between Bob Fitzsimmons and Peter Maher on a sandbar in the Rio Grande, just beyond U.S. lawmen's reach. Fans came by special train and packed the Jersey Lilly. Fitzsimmons knocked Maher out in the first round, in under two minutes. Newspaper coverage made Bean nationally famous.

folsom.name: Folsom Train Robberies
folsom.summary: Ketchum's gang hit the same train twice. Lay was captured; Black Jack was wounded and caught on a solo attempt.

four-dead.name: Four Dead in Five Seconds
four-dead.summary: Marshal Stoudenmire's famous street gunfight on El Paso Street.

frisco-shootout.name: Frisco Shootout
frisco-shootout.summary: Elfego Baca held off a large group of cowboys from a small hut for some 33 hours.

goodnight-loving-first-drive.name: Goodnight and Loving's First Drive Sets Out
goodnight-loving-first-drive.summary: Charles Goodnight and Oliver Loving left near Fort Belknap with about 2,000 Longhorns and 18 cowhands, including Bose Ikard and 'One-Armed' Bill Wilson, on the drive that blazed the Goodnight-Loving Trail to Fort Sumner, New Mexico.

hardin-killed.name: Killing of John Wesley Hardin
hardin-killed.summary: John Selman shot Hardin in the Acme Saloon while he was rolling dice.

heath-lynching.name: Lynching of John Heath
heath-lynching.place: Second and Toughnut Streets, Tombstone, AZ
heath-lynching.summary: Angry that Heath got life in prison instead of the gallows, a mob of miners took him from the Tombstone jail and hanged him from a telegraph pole.

hickok-killed.name: Killing of Wild Bill Hickok
hickok-killed.summary: Jack McCall shot Hickok in the back of the head during a poker game in Saloon No. 10.

hickok-tutt.name: Hickok–Tutt Shootout
hickok-tutt.summary: Often called the first Wild West showdown. Tutt wore Hickok's pocket watch, held over a gambling debt, onto the town square; the two faced off and Hickok shot him through the heart. Hickok was acquitted on grounds of self-defense, and the fight made him famous.

holbrook-shootout.name: Owens–Blevins Shootout
holbrook-shootout.summary: Serving a warrant at the Blevins house, Sheriff Owens killed three men and wounded a fourth.

ingalls.name: Battle of Ingalls
ingalls.summary: Deputy marshals raided the Doolin gang's hideout town; three lawmen died.

iron-springs.name: Gunfight at Iron Springs
iron-springs.summary: Wyatt Earp killed Curly Bill Brocius with a shotgun at a water hole.

jesse-killed.name: Assassination of Jesse James
jesse-killed.summary: Bob Ford shot Jesse James in the back of the head while Jesse straightened a picture.

juneau-wharf.name: Shootout on Juneau Wharf
juneau-wharf.summary: Soapy Smith and guard Frank Reid shot each other; Smith died on the spot.

kid-killed.name: Death of Billy the Kid
kid-killed.summary: Garrett shot the Kid in a darkened bedroom at Pete Maxwell's house.

lincoln-county-war.name: Lincoln County War
lincoln-county-war.summary: A feud between 'The House' (Lawrence Murphy and James Dolan's store, which controlled local trade and was backed by Sheriff William Brady and the Santa Fe Ring) and newcomers John Tunstall and Alexander McSween, with John Chisum's support. It began when a sheriff's posse killed Tunstall on Feb 18, 1878. His hands formed the Regulators, Billy the Kid among them, and revenge killings followed: Morton and Baker (March), Sheriff Brady (April 1), Blazer's Mill (April 4), and the five-day Battle of Lincoln in July, where McSween was killed. About 19 people died. It is usually considered over by early 1879, though some date its end to the Kid's death in 1881.

loving-dies.name: Death of Oliver Loving
loving-dies.summary: Wounded weeks earlier when a Comanche war party trapped him on the Pecos River, Oliver Loving died of gangrene at Fort Sumner. Goodnight later carried his body home to Weatherford, Texas.

morgan-earp-killing.name: Assassination of Morgan Earp
morgan-earp-killing.summary: Shot through a window while playing billiards. Stilwell and Spence were among the suspects.

northfield-raid.name: Northfield Raid
northfield-raid.summary: Armed townspeople broke up the bank robbery; the Youngers were captured days later.

ok-corral.name: Gunfight at the O.K. Corral
ok-corral.summary: About 30 seconds of gunfire left Billy Clanton and both McLaurys dead; Virgil and Morgan Earp were wounded.

pearl-hart-robbery.name: Globe–Florence Stage Robbery
pearl-hart-robbery.summary: Pearl Hart and Joe Boot robbed one of the last stagecoaches held up in the West.

roscoe.name: Roscoe Gun Battle
roscoe.summary: Pinkerton agents and a deputy met the Younger brothers on the road; John Younger was killed.

round-rock.name: Round Rock Shootout
round-rock.summary: Texas Rangers ambushed Sam Bass, tipped off by gang member Jim Murphy. Bass died two days later.

royal-gorge-war.name: Royal Gorge War: Pueblo Roundhouse Standoff
royal-gorge-war.place: Pueblo, CO (Royal Gorge / Cañon City area)
royal-gorge-war.summary: The Santa Fe and the Denver & Rio Grande railroads fought from 1878 to 1880 over the narrow Royal Gorge route to the Leadville silver boom. With the case in court, the Santa Fe hired Bat Masterson, then Ford County sheriff, to raise a 'posse.' Doc Holliday helped him recruit about 60 men, including Dirty Dave Rudabaugh, Ben Thompson and Mysterious Dave Mather. On June 11, 1879 they held the Santa Fe roundhouse in Pueblo, with a borrowed cannon. Rio Grande men took back depots up and down the line, and the roundhouse ended without a real battle; one account says a D&RG official paid Masterson's men to leave. Shots were exchanged at some stations, and historians disagree on how many died. The railroads settled with the 'Treaty of Boston' (Mar 27, 1880): the Rio Grande got the gorge and paid the Santa Fe about $1.8 million for its work there.

san-vicente.name: Shootout at San Vicente
san-vicente.summary: Bolivian soldiers surrounded two American bandits, generally believed to be Butch and Sundance.

sanderson-robbery.name: Sanderson Train Robbery
sanderson-robbery.summary: Express messenger David Trousdale killed Ben Kilpatrick with an ice mallet.

scouts-of-the-prairie.name: "The Scouts of the Prairie" Debuts
scouts-of-the-prairie.summary: Ned Buntline put real frontier scouts on stage. Buffalo Bill and Texas Jack played themselves, and Giuseppina Morlacchi co-starred. Critics panned it, but the 1872–73 season was a hit and planted the seed for Buffalo Bill's Wild West.

short-courtright.name: Luke Short–Jim Courtright Gunfight
short-courtright.summary: A rare face-to-face street duel. Short killed Courtright outside the White Elephant Saloon.

stinking-springs.name: Capture at Stinking Springs
stinking-springs.summary: Pat Garrett's posse killed Charlie Bowdre and captured Billy the Kid and Dave Rudabaugh.

tascosa-big-fight.name: Big Fight at the Jenkins Saloon
tascosa-big-fight.summary: LS Ranch cowboys fought rustlers of 'The System' outside the Dunn & Jenkins Saloon after bartender Lem Woodruff shot LS man Ed King. Four men died, including King, Frank Valley, Fred Chilton and bystander Jesse Sheets; all were buried on Tascosa's Boot Hill.

tom-horn-hanged.name: Hanging of Tom Horn
tom-horn-hanged.summary: Horn was hanged for the killing of 14-year-old Willie Nickell, a conviction still argued over.

tunstall-killing.name: Murder of John Tunstall
tunstall-killing.place: Near the Rio Feliz, Lincoln County, NM
tunstall-killing.summary: The killing that started the Lincoln County War. A sheriff's posse, sent by Sheriff Brady to seize Tunstall's horses over a debt claim against his partner McSween, caught up with the 24-year-old Englishman as he and his hands drove horses toward Lincoln. Deputy William Morton, Jesse Evans, Tom Hill and Frank Baker were named as the killers; Tunstall was shot in the head, officially for 'resisting arrest.' Billy the Kid and Dick Brewer were among his hands that day.

vaudeville.name: Vaudeville Theater Ambush
vaudeville.summary: Thompson and Fisher were shot dead in the theater's balcony.

vendetta-ride.name: Earp Vendetta Ride
vendetta-ride.summary: Wyatt Earp's posse killed Frank Stilwell, Curly Bill and others blamed for Morgan's murder.

wilcox.name: Wilcox Train Robbery
wilcox.summary: The Wild Bunch dynamited a Union Pacific express car. Butch Cassidy's part is debated.

windy-cahill-shooting.name: Billy the Kid Shoots Windy Cahill
windy-cahill-shooting.place: Atkins' Cantina, Bonita (near Camp Grant), AZ
windy-cahill-shooting.summary: The Kid's first killing. Then going by Henry Antrim ('Kid Antrim'), he was playing poker at George Atkins' cantina when blacksmith Frank 'Windy' Cahill called him a pimp. The Kid called Cahill an SOB, and Cahill threw him to the floor and pinned him. The Kid got to his pistol and shot Cahill in the stomach. Cahill gave a deathbed statement and died Aug 18. A coroner's jury called it 'criminal and unjustifiable.' The Kid was held in the Camp Grant guardhouse, escaped, and fled to New Mexico, where he soon began calling himself William H. Bonney.

chisholm-trail.aka: McCoy Trail, Eastern Trail, Abilene Trail
chisholm-trail.cattle: Commonly estimated at about 5 million head; some 700,000 reached the Kansas railheads in 1871 alone
chisholm-trail.end: Abilene, KS (later Ellsworth, Wichita and Caldwell)
chisholm-trail.history:
In 1867 Illinois cattle buyer Joseph McCoy built stockyards at Abilene, Kansas, on the Kansas Pacific Railway, west of the farm settlements that had blocked the Shawnee Trail. That year O.W. Wheeler and his partners drove a herd of about 2,400 steers north from San Antonio. In Indian Territory they found the wagon ruts of trader Jesse Chisholm's road near the North Canadian River and followed them toward Kansas. Other herds followed, and over time drovers applied Chisholm's name to the whole route from Texas; the name first shows up in newspapers around 1869.

Herds came up from South Texas through Austin, Waco and Fort Worth, crossed the Red River at Red River Station and pushed across Indian Territory roughly where U.S. Highway 81 runs today. As the quarantine line and the farmers moved west, the trail's end moved with them: Abilene until 1871, then Ellsworth and Wichita, and finally Caldwell into the mid-1880s. The trail drives produced the cattle towns, the gunfights and the cowboy legend the ledger is full of. Wild Bill Hickok and Tom 'Bear River' Smith policed Abilene because of it.

What exactly counts as 'the Chisholm Trail' is still argued. Historians Gary and Margaret Kraisinger argue the name properly belongs only to the route through Indian Territory and Kansas, and that the Texas feeder routes had other names. By 1876 most Texas herds had moved west to the Great Western Trail and Dodge City.
chisholm-trail.name: Chisholm Trail
chisholm-trail.namedFor: Jesse Chisholm, a Scottish-Cherokee trader whose wagon road through Indian Territory the cattle drovers followed. He never drove cattle and died in 1868, before the name caught on.
chisholm-trail.notes: Not named for John Chisum, the New Mexico cattle king, though the two names are often confused. Thornton Chisholm, a Texas drover who took a herd north in 1866, is also sometimes credited.

goodnight-loving-trail.cattle: First drive: about 2,000 Longhorns with 18 cowhands
goodnight-loving-trail.end: Fort Sumner, NM, later Denver, CO and Cheyenne, WY
goodnight-loving-trail.history:
In 1866 the Army had thousands of Navajos and Mescalero Apaches confined at the Bosque Redondo reservation near Fort Sumner, New Mexico, and needed beef. Charles Goodnight and Oliver Loving combined their herds, and on June 6, 1866, they left near Fort Belknap, Texas, with about 2,000 Longhorns and 18 men, including Bose Ikard and 'One-Armed' Bill Wilson. To avoid Comanche country they went southwest along the old Butterfield stage route, across an 80-mile waterless stretch to Horsehead Crossing on the Pecos, then north up the river to Fort Sumner. The Army paid them $12,000 in gold.

Loving took the rest of the herd on to Colorado while Goodnight went back for more. In 1867 Comanches attacked the drive near Horsehead Crossing. Loving and Wilson rode ahead and were trapped by a war party on the Pecos. Loving, badly wounded, made it to Fort Sumner but died there of gangrene on September 25, 1867. Goodnight later carried his body back to Texas for burial, the story that inspired 'Lonesome Dove.'

Goodnight kept using the route and extended it north through Colorado to the Union Pacific at Cheyenne, Wyoming. Biographer J. Evetts Haley noted that the leg to Fort Sumner was usually called the Goodnight Trail and the longer route the Goodnight-Loving Trail, though the names were used interchangeably.
goodnight-loving-trail.name: Goodnight-Loving Trail
goodnight-loving-trail.namedFor: Cattlemen Charles Goodnight and Oliver Loving, who blazed it together in 1866.
goodnight-loving-trail.notes: Some historians argue John Chisum and others drove cattle across West Texas and up the Pecos before Goodnight and Loving, and an 1897 map labels part of the route 'the Chisum Trail.'

great-western-trail.aka: Western Trail, Fort Griffin Trail, Dodge City Trail, Old Texas Trail
great-western-trail.cattle: By 1876 it carried most northbound Texas herds; 73,000–108,000 head passed Fort Griffin that year
great-western-trail.end: Dodge City, KS and Ogallala, NE, with branches to Montana, the Dakotas and Canada
great-western-trail.history:
In 1874 John T. Lytle drove 3,500 Longhorns from South Texas to Nebraska on a new route west of the settled country. It ran from Bandera through Albany and Fort Griffin, where the herds watered and resupplied, crossed the Red River at Doan's Crossing and passed Camp Supply in Indian Territory to Dodge City. Kansas's 1875 quarantine law closed the eastern railheads, and by 1876 most Texas herds had switched to this route.

The trail fed the wildest years of Fort Griffin and Dodge City; the cowboys who came up it are the 'Texans came to town' in half the stories in this ledger. From Dodge it continued north to the Union Pacific at Ogallala, Nebraska, and herds went on from there to stock new ranches in Wyoming, Montana and the Dakotas, as far as Canada. A western branch connected Tascosa and the XIT Ranch to Dodge City until 1885.

Quarantine laws against Texas fever, barbed wire and the spread of railroads into Texas wore it down after 1885, and the last herds went up in the early 1890s.
great-western-trail.length: The longest of the Texas cattle trails
great-western-trail.name: Great Western Cattle Trail
great-western-trail.namedFor: Not a person: it was simply the 'Western' trail, west of the Chisholm. Drovers also named it for the places it led, Fort Griffin and Dodge City.
great-western-trail.notes: Sources differ on where it started; most point to Bandera.

shawnee-trail.aka: Texas Road, Sedalia Trail, Kansas Trail
shawnee-trail.end: Sedalia, MO and Baxter Springs, KS
shawnee-trail.history:
Texans were driving cattle and horses north along the old Texas Road through Indian Territory by the 1840s, headed for markets in Missouri. Drovers just called it 'the trail,' the Sedalia Trail or the Kansas Trail; by the late 1850s the name Shawnee Trail had come into general use, though nobody knows exactly why. North of Fort Gibson it split into branches ending at Baxter Springs, Kansas, and at Sedalia, Kansas City, Independence and St. Louis in Missouri.

The trouble was Texas fever, a tick-borne disease the Longhorns carried but were immune to. It killed the farmers' cattle wherever the herds passed. Missouri banned Texas cattle in 1855, and armed bands of farmers turned herds back. The Civil War shut the trail down almost completely.

When the war ended, beef worth a few dollars a head in Texas was worth many times that up north, and in 1866 an estimated 200,000 to 260,000 head started up the Shawnee Trail for the railhead at Sedalia. Many never got there: farmers in Missouri and Kansas met the herds with guns and quarantine laws, and drovers were robbed, beaten and turned back. The next year Joseph McCoy opened stockyards at Abilene, Kansas, west of the settlements, and most of the traffic moved west to the Chisholm Trail. Drives on the Shawnee continued on a smaller scale until about 1873.
shawnee-trail.name: Shawnee Trail
shawnee-trail.namedFor: No one knows for sure. Probably a Shawnee village on the Texas side of the Red River near the crossing, or the Shawnee Hills in Indian Territory.
